#5017. Claude Fable 5.5, GPT 6.2 Astra Could Be Right Around the Corner, Leaks Suggest

Claude Fable 5.5, GPT 6.2 Astra Could Be Right Around the Corner, Leaks Suggest

Users on X say Anthropic is quietly testing an unreleased version of Mythos and Fable, and OpenAI is about to launch GPT 6.2 Astra.

Nobody has confirmed anything but the rumors are based on a handful of showcase demos, plus a catalog entry and a hidden website label that were both removed soon after appearing.

Fable is the top commercial tier of Claude, the chatbot that competes with ChatGPT, and the priciest flagship Anthropic sells for writing software and handling office work. Mythos is a restricted model that Anthropic offers to a select group of clients, including government and cyber giants due to its capabilities.

Anthropic filed for an IPO, its first sale of shares to the public, on October 26, reporting $16.29 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026 against $1.16 billion a year earlier.

Anthropic launched Fable 5 on June 9, pulled it offline for 18 days under U.S. export controls, which are government limits on who may use a technology, and released Fable 5.1 on September 1. Opus 5.5 followed on September 22, and Anthropic says it performs at the level of Fable 5.1 on most tasks at a fraction of the price.

The chatter began on October 1, when users posted screenshots of Claude still labeled Fable 5.1 beside outputs they said looked stronger. On October 11, pseudonymous user Chetaslua, known for sharing insights on unreleased models and spotting changes in outputs, logs and other signals of new models before they are officially announced, wrote that “Claude Opus 5.5 is routing to a new model,” adding that it could be either Fable 5.5 or a new Opus model.

🚨 Claude Opus 5.5 is routing to a new model < this can be fable 5.5 or new opus i have no idea >

Drew every frame of this animation using JS. The life of a Human

Two Prompts : literally 4 lines Time : 2 HoursTokens : 27 Miliion Thinking Effort : Max pic.twitter.com/6Uy9qxQV7e

— Chetaslua (@chetaslua) October 11, 2026

Routing means a request is quietly sent to a different model behind the scenes. Some users suspect an A/B test, in which Anthropic shows a new version to a slice of users to compare it with the current one while the screen keeps the old name.

“Is this Fable 5.5? Saw posts that Opus is routed to Fable 5.5, so I decided to make a complex 2D animation with it,” AI developer Shikhar—known for vibe coding a Spiderman game that went viral on social media—wrote on X, next to an animation made with Opus, but with a superior quality compared to what the model usually outputs.

Min Choi, another reputable leaker in the AI community, listed the clip in a roundup of examples: “A 30-second Spider-Verse-style 2D animation: a character on a city street, then a web-swing over the rooftops.” Shikhar posed the model as a question rather than a finding, but the timing helped feed the FOMO.

10. A 30-second Spider-Verse-style 2D animation: a character on a city street, then a web-swing over the rooftops.

He says it's one HTML file (WebGL, GLSL shaders and 2D Canvas), made with Opus while it was reportedly routing to Fable 5.5. He asks "Is this Fable 5.5?" himself.…

On October 13, an automated update to LiteLLM, an open-source tool developers use to connect to many AI providers, added an entry named “claude-fable-5-5” after Microsoft’s Azure cloud catalog listed it as generally available. The entry copied its price and limits from Fable 5.1, its notes say no source states a price, capability or text-length limit for Fable 5.5, and it was later removed.

“Mythos 5.5 is already listed HTML source code of Anthropic’s official website,” Kim Isenberg—who also goes by the pseudonymous "Chubby," and is one of the most active and followed accounts in the AI community—wrote on Sunday alongside a screenshot of the code behind Anthropic’s Mythos page. “Thanks to the anonymous person who sent me the tip via email,” the account posted.

Mythos is the restricted twin of Fable, the same underlying model with lighter safety filters, reserved for vetted cybersecurity and biology researchers.

Mythos 5.5 is already listed HTML source code of Anthropic's official website

Thanks to the anonymous person who sent me the tip via email 🙂 pic.twitter.com/HqCPUD3inP

— Chubby♨️ (@kimmonismus) November 1, 2026

Chetaslua counted six appearances of the label in the page’s hidden code, in an invisible headline and in the alt text of the logo, the description attached to an image for screen readers. A check of the live page on Monday showed only Mythos 5.1, the version Anthropic released alongside Fable 5.1 in September.

OpenAI also has its own share of AI FOMO.

“OpenAI is quietly A/B testing a new variant called GPT-6.2 Astra, and it’s already showing up in Codex usage analytics,” a user known as TokenGremlin wrote on Sunday. “The model picker still says GPT-6 Astra, but the usage breakdown for some accounts now lists gpt-6.2-astra separately.”

OpenAI is quietly A/B testing a new variant called GPT-6.2 Astra, and it's already showing up in Codex usage analytics.

The model picker still says GPT-6 Astra, but the usage breakdown for some accounts now lists gpt-6.2-astra separately. Multiple users are seeing the exact same… pic.twitter.com/XAmFfL27m6

— Token Gremlin (@TokenGremlin) November 1, 2026

Codex is OpenAI’s coding assistant, and a screenshot circulating on X showed gpt-6.2-astra at 19.8% of one account’s usage, next to gpt-6-astra at 80%. OpenAI has not announced a 6.2 model, and it released GPT-6 Astra on September 3.

“GPT-6.2 Astra is already showing up in codex usage analytics, as per Token Gremlin,” Chubby wrote, predicting a release “very soon, in response to Fable 5.5 and Anthropic’s IPO.”

“Next week is going to be exciting,” Chubby wrote.

Anthropic’s S-1, the registration document a company files with U.S. regulators before selling shares, lists the Nasdaq ticker ANT and names Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley first among its underwriters, the banks that sell the shares to investors. The share count and price range are still blank.

Because Anthropic first filed confidentially in June, SEC rules require the paperwork to be public for 15 days before the roadshow, the marketing tour where banks pitch the shares to investors, which puts the earliest start at November 10.

#5014. From Uptober to Hacktober: Are Bitcoin’s seasonal patterns becoming obsolete?

Bitcoin lost 7.3% in October 2026 after another decline the previous year, despite the month’s historically strong returns, as analysts reassess seasonal signals.

Bitcoin’s back-to-back October losses have put its “Uptober” reputation under the microscope as analysts weigh seasonal trends against institutional demand and economic conditions.

Bitcoin fell 7.3% in October 2026, following a roughly 4% decline a year earlier, according to CoinGlass data.

The losses defied October’s historically bullish reputation, which earned it the nickname “Uptober.” This year, industry figures turned to darker labels, including “Black October” and “Hacktober,” amid a wave of crypto security incidents, including Binance’s record-breaking $6.3 billion hack.

October has historically delivered Bitcoin’s highest median return at 15.4%, with gains in 10 of 13 years through 2025, according to Andrew Yang, a researcher at crypto analytics firm Kaiko.

September’s historically bearish reputation has weakened as well. Bitcoin has posted gains every September since 2023, which could reflect traders buying ahead of an expected October rally, Yang told Cointelegraph.

Median monthly Bitcoin return by calendar month since January 2013. Source: Kaiko

Bitcoin’s narrowing price swings may also be making seasonal trends less pronounced, Yang said. Its typical monthly move has declined from 14% between 2013 and 2016 to 9.6% since 2024, leaving less room for sharp seasonal rallies, he added.

Analysts also pointed to institutional investment and broader economic conditions as increasingly important influences on Bitcoin’s price.

Justin d’Anethan, head of research at Arctic Digital, pointed to exchange-traded fund (ETF) flows and corporate Bitcoin buyers, saying their investment decisions are shaped more by liquidity, interest rates and investment mandates than seasonal trading narratives.

Related: Bitcoin ETF flows give mixed read on institutional demand: CoinShares

US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $515 million in net outflows in October, while spot Ether ETFs saw a record $1.61 billion in monthly withdrawals.

Yang cautioned that spot Bitcoin ETFs, approved in January 2024, are too recent to assess. Still, Bitcoin “increasingly trades like a macro asset, driven more by economic data and institutional flows than by the calendar,” he said.

Despite two consecutive October losses, analysts cautioned against writing off Uptober entirely.

Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant, said October has generally performed better during Bitcoin bull markets and worse during bear markets, making the broader market cycle an important factor when comparing returns.

“Price performance depends more on spot demand dynamics than cyclical patterns, and demand doesn’t care about the calendar,” Moreno told Cointelegraph.

Related: Bitcoin risks worst October in 12 years as tech sell-off spreads to gold

Markus Levin, co-founder of XYO, said that traders may be anticipating seasonal gains earlier. “When enough people expect a rally in October, the rally gets priced in before the month arrives,” he said.

“Uptober has historical validity but, like other seasonality metrics, it can also fail at times,” said Arctic Digital’s d’Anethan.

Magazine: Cybersecurity’s Black October: How to protect yourself

#5013. Binance hackers begin swapping stolen Solana tokens for Bitcoin: Chainalysis

Crypto exchange Gate said it froze two linked accounts as US investigators urged platforms to block transactions tied to the $6.3 billion theft.

The hackers behind Binance’s $6.3 billion theft have begun converting stolen Solana tokens into Bitcoin after largely emptying the wallets used to launder funds on Tron, according to blockchain investigators.

Lookonchain reported Sunday that the hackers had moved 486,970 Solana (SOL) tokens, worth about $46.4 million, and were swapping them for Bitcoin (BTC) through Relay.

The activity involves funds that escaped the freezes imposed after Thursday’s theft, the largest in cryptocurrency history. Industry partners, including Tether and Circle, froze about $3 billion in stolen assets, while investigator SomaXBT estimated the attackers still controlled about $3.5 billion.

Binance said the attack compromised its hot wallets, with early findings pointing to a hacked employee laptop before investigators identified additional breach points. The exchange began restoring withdrawals Sunday, pledged to cover the losses and has been working with US authorities to trace and recover the stolen assets.

Related: OKX draws $445M in net inflows as Binance outflows exceed $7B

Chainalysis said Sunday that most of the hackers’ temporary holding wallets on Tron had been emptied as laundering activity expanded to Solana. It put the value of the Tron transfers at about $500 million.

The $500 million figure counted transfers during laundering, including repeated movements between wallets, SomaXBT said in response. About $242 million actually left the Tron holding wallets, he said.

Chainalysis said Friday that hackers may be using automation to obscure the trail, citing thousands of transactions in a short period. The firm observed funds circulating repeatedly between wallets, sometimes returning to addresses used earlier in the sequence.

Some stolen funds also reached centralized exchange Gate. Lookonchain reported Monday that the hackers had deposited about $250,000 there over the preceding 12 hours.

Gate subsequently said it had frozen two linked accounts and would cooperate with law enforcement. Its statement did not specify how much money was frozen.

The FBI on Saturday attributed Thursday’s theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers and published wallet addresses linked to the stolen assets.

The agency, US Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation urged THORChain node operators, exchanges and decentralized finance (DeFi) services to block transactions involving those addresses or funds traced back to them.

Investigators had observed the hackers converting stolen assets primarily into Ether (ETH) and expected further laundering through DeFi and instant swap services, the FBI said.

#5012. Melatonin Is Not Just for Sleep

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Melatonin is widely known as the substance that makes us sleepy. It is commonly used as an over-the-counter sleep aid to treat jet lag and bouts of insomnia. However, new research shows that melatonin plays a wider role in maintaining overall health. Melatonin is a potent antioxidant that can prevent tissue damage. Evidence suggests it could help ward off certain types of cancer (Proietti, Reiter & Bizzarriet, 2012). It plays an essential role in the immune system’s ability to fight infections and heal from injuries (Szataniak & Packi, 2025; Singh et al., 2024).

Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is known as a chronobiotic hormone, which means that it regulates circadian rhythm. Tryptophan, an amino acid ingested from certain foods, serves as a building block for the production of serotonin. Serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood regulation, is converted to melatonin primarily in the brain’s pineal gland. Production of melatonin is increased during darkness at night and it is released directly into the bloodstream. Levels decline during the day as production is inhibited by light (Kamfar et al., 2024).

Sleep has long been known to promote healing. People need extra sleep to recover from physical ailments. Research published in 2025 by Szataniak et al. showed that immune responses are strongly affected by the sleep cycle. The authors analysed 59 studies published from 2000-2025 that examined how melatonin production affects the immune system. They found that chronic sleep deprivation impairs immune response which increases susceptibility to infections and inflammation (Szataniak, et al 2025).

Pro-inflammatory molecules of the immune system, called cytokines, mobilize aggressive responses to fight off viruses, infections or foreign pathogens. This process is most active during sleep. Elevated levels of cytokines during infections or inflammation promote increased sleepiness associated with illness. This is an adaptive response and serves to promote recovery (Singh et al., 2024).

In 2024, Singh et al. published results that showed decreased melatonin levels correlate with increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines. They found that chronic sleep deprivation increases cytokine production, contributing to systemic low-grade inflammation. This imbalance potentially increases the risk for cardiovascular disease, cancer, atherosclerosis, diabetes, and autoimmune illnesses (Szataniak et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2024). Chronic elevation of these cytokines has also been found to be associated with fatigue and immunosuppression (Szataniak et al., 2025).

Another component of the immune response acts to quiet the system and heal from inflammation and infections. Anti-inflammatory molecules such as the hormone cortisol are enhanced during wakefulness and play an essential role in regulating sleep and immune function (Singh et al., 2024). Cortisol reduces inflammation in the body and has immunosuppressant effects. It increases the sense of alertness, and like melatonin it is released following a circadian rhythm (Hoyt, Zeiders, Ehrlich & Adam, 2016). Levels of cortisol are highest early in the morning and decrease throughout the day. During sleep, cortisol levels are decreased while melatonin levels are increased. Chronic sleep deprivation can disrupt cortisol secretion, leading to a negative impact on immunity and susceptibility to infections (Singh et al., 2024).

Getting enough sleep is essential for maintaining physical health. Screening for insomnia should be included in routine healthcare visits. Education and increased awareness regarding the importance of adequate sleep should be part of health and wellness initiatives (Szataniak et al., 2025). Recently, enhanced widespread screening for pain issues and depression have been incorporated into medical visits. This should be expanded to include regular sleep assessments.

Evidence supports the use of dietary supplements containing melatonin or its precursor tryptophan to treat certain types of short-term sleep disruption (Szataniak et al., 2025; American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 2021). However, melatonin supplementation is not recommended as a long-term strategy for treatment of chronic insomnia (AASM, 2021). The American Academy of Sleep Medicine emphasizes the importance of assessing underlying causes of insomnia. They recommend implementing behavioral routines to improve sleep. Collectively referred to as sleep hygiene, this includes strategies such as turning off electronic devices (for example phones, television, and computers) 30 to 60 minutes before bed, adhering to a consistent sleep schedule, and caution around substances such as caffeine and alcohol.

About 10% of adults meet criteria for chronic insomnia disorder (AASM, 2021). In these cases, a course of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia or CBT-I is recommended. Medications for insomnia are generally considered a last resort after behavioral options have been implemented (AASM, 2021).

More recent research presented at the 2025 American Heart Association conference examined long-term melatonin use in 130,828 adults diagnosed with insomnia. Results showed that the use of melatonin for 12 months or more was correlated with an increased likelihood of being diagnosed with heart failure or dying from any cause over the course of five years. Although cause and effect was not proven, it highlights potential cardiovascular risks and the need for further research to establish the safety of long-term melatonin use (American Heart Association, 2025).

Hormones, including melatonin, are part of a complex endocrine system that exert multiple effects on different organs. Maintaining balance promotes resilience and wellness. Adequate sleep is a critical component to maintaining long-term health and optimal immune function. (Singh et al., 2024).

American Academy of Sleep Medicine, Missing the mark with melatonin: Finding the best treatment for insomnia (2021). https://aasm.org/missing-the-mark-melatonin-finding-best-treatment-insomnia/

American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, Long-term use of melatonin supplements to support sleep may have negative health effects (2025). Abstract MP 2306. https://newsroom.heart.org/news/long-term-use-of-melatonin-supplements-to-support-sleep-may-have-negative-health-effects

Hoyt, L., Zeiders, K.H., Ehrlich, K.B., Adam, E.K., (2016). Positive upshots of cortisol in everyday life. Emotion 16(4):431-435.

Kamfar, W.W., Khraiwesh, H.M., Ibrahim, M.O., Qadhi, A.H., Azhar, W.F., Ghafouri, K.J., Alhussain, M.H., Aldairi, A.A., AlShahrani, A.M., Alghannam, A.F., Abdulal, R.H., Al-Slaihat, A.H., Qutob, M.S., Elrggal, M.E., Ghaith, M.M., Azzeh, FS (2024). Comprehensive review of melatonin as a promising nutritional and nutraceutical supplement. Heliyon Vol 10(2).

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e24266

Proietti, S., Cucina, A., Reiter, R.J., Bizzarri, M., (2012). Molecular mechanisms of melatonin’s inhibitory actions on breast cancers. Cell Mol Life Sci 70(12): 2139-21-57. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00018-012-1161-8

#5010. I Didn't Expect to Love This Prada Cologne. But This Is Why It's My Go-To Fall Scent

Prada Paradigme looks loud. The cologne inside is surprisingly refined.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHEN PRADA PARADIGME Eau de Parfum was released last year, the first thing I noticed was the bottle. It has a stark lime-green-and-black design that can best be described as Green Goblin chic, which is ironic considering Spider-Man himself, Tom Holland, fronts its campaign. The fragrance itself, however, is no joke. I dug the scent so much, I quickly featured it at the top of my next new releases column before giving it a 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Award.

Prada clearly felt similarly, as it dropped a more concentrated Prada Paradigme Le Parfum this May. After wearing the OG cologne regularly for over a year, I can confirm my early impression of it wasn’t t misguided. Here’s how the Eau de Parfum performed over 12 months and how the new Le Parfum stacks up.

At its core, Paradigme is an amber-woody cologne, which is definitely up my alley. But it’s also bold and spicy—two cologne descriptors I tend to avoid. Paradigme pulls off hitting this intersection of vibes with a scent profile that is refined and powerful yet still grounded and casual.

It opens with a warm blend of Peru balsam, benzoin resin, and guaiac wood before settling into a musky finish with some hints of citrusy bergamot and rose. There’s also a lingering bourbon note that I especially appreciate as someone who loves the smell (and taste) of whiskey. In the Le Parfum, the citrus and floral notes come through a bit clearer and definitely stick around longer. But it has the same rich amber-woody base.

To me, this is ideal for wear at a low-lit cocktail bar, that’s potentially haunted in the best possible way. In short, this is what I’d wear if I was hitting up Overlook Hotel’s bar in Stephen King’s The Shining—not to be confused with the Stanley Hotel in Colorado, on which that hotel is based, which I have visited and wore something lighter at (it’s pretty tight in there). Prada Paradigme Le Parfum, on the other hand, is better suited for wandering around the Overlook’s extensive hedge maze.

This more concentrated iteration is best suited for spring and summer, as its deeper floral notes could clash with the cozy vibe of fall and winter. While the EDP is best-suited for the cooler, moodier months, I dig it when temps are high too. There’s enough bergamot and rose in there to reflect the brightness of the season, and the guaiac wood gives it a slight earthy edge that works well during the warmer months. I’m also someone who gladly enjoys sipping on bourbon when it’s 90 degrees out, so my view may be skewed.

After applying the cologne with two to three sprays to my neck, I get about eight to nine hours of quality wear. The Le Parfum lasts about an hour longer and maintains its intensity more strongly than the EDP. It also builds more in intensity over the first couple of hours before plateauing, whereas the EDP settles after about 45 minutes and stays consistent for the next few hours. I usually stick to two sprays with the Le Parfum, as the projection is stronger.

Prada Paradigme Eau de Parfum strikes a rare balance between bold and easygoing, blending amber woods, spice, bergamot, rose, and bourbon. It feels refined without being stuffy, works across seasons, and lasts roughly eight to nine hours on my skin—making it an easy everyday fragrance with enough personality for nights out. If you’re looking for something stronger and slightly spicier, Prada Paradigme Le Parfum is the pick. It lasts longer, but the scent isn’t as well-suited for year-round wear as the OG.

#5009. FATF targets crypto hubs in review of money laundering controls

The watchdog has not named the jurisdictions under review. Initial findings on compliance with its crypto standards are due in June 2027.

Update (Nov. 3, 2026, 7:35 am UTC): This article has been updated to include comments from an FATF spokesperson and additional details from its July 2026 report.

The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) is launching a targeted review of jurisdictions with significant crypto activity to address gaps in how governments apply global anti-money laundering standards.

On Friday, the FATF, an intergovernmental body that sets global standards to combat money laundering, announced that the review would focus primarily on jurisdictions with “materially important” virtual asset service provider (VASP) activity, taking their existing assessment status into account.

A  FATF spokesperson pointed to its July 2026 report, which lists FATF members and other jurisdictions with significant VASP activity. Jurisdictions in the table, including the US, UK, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates account for about 97% of the global virtual asset market.

The spokesperson did not confirm which jurisdictions from the existing list would be selected. Initial findings will be published in June 2027, with further results in October 2027.

For non-member jurisdictions, inclusion in the table requires a more than 0.25% of global crypto trading volume or a top-30 ranking for crypto ownership and adoption.

Inclusion in the table does not indicate a jurisdiction’s illicit finance risk or compliance with FATF standards.

The July report found that 83% of surveyed jurisdictions had adopted crypto Travel Rule legislation, while significant enforcement gaps persisted.

The Travel Rule requires crypto service providers to share information about the sender and recipient of transfers.

The report found that 55 of the 91 jurisdictions with Travel Rule laws had yet to take supervisory or enforcement action over compliance.

Authorities also struggled to identify unlicensed crypto businesses and oversee providers serving local customers from overseas.

Related: FATF urges faster crypto AML enforcement as stablecoin crime increases

#5008. In Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick’s North Carolina Home, Southern Hospitality Meets Modern Charm

The home was, decidedly, not love at first sight for Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick. “One of the rooms had caved in; there was water pouring in through the ceiling,” Decker says of the first time the couple saw the Charlotte, North Carolina, Georgian-style house.

But even in its dilapidated state, the 1960s-era home was still intriguing: It was located in the favored neighborhood for the young family, and its traditional, elegant proportions were still evident through its disrepair. At first it was Roddick, the former number-one men’s singles tennis player, who urged Decker to keep the house on their short list. Soon model and actor Decker, who grew up in nearby Matthews, warmed at the chance to rehabilitate a proper Carolina home with details like dental crown molding and classic brick. “We’d moved so many times [before this house],” she says. “And we were excited to try something new. For us, that meant a historic house with some old Southern bones.”

In the entry, Roddick is seated on a vintage sofa covered in a Zak and Fox fabric. Decker stands next to the walnut staircase built by Masterpiece Staircase and finished by Tony Montognese. The custom chandelier is by Kalin Asenov, the rug is vintage, and the artwork is by Kieran Brennan Hinton.

The family’s living room, clad in mahogany paneling, is Decker and Roddick’s favorite space in the whole home. The fireplace was designed by Decker, fabricated by Tyler Ernsberger, and stained by Tony Montognese, with animal carvings done by Stan Dunham. The 1930s coffee table is by Paul László, and the light fixture is a vintage Longobard for Poliarte. The chairs, clockwise from top right, are by BDDW, vintage Swedish sourced from PRB Collection, and a vintage Guglielmo Ulrich.

The home’s foyer received the biggest glow-up, with the staircase being entirely redesigned from a curving one. Chandelier and flush-mount light designed by Decker and Kalin Asenov, sideboard by BDDW, the mirror and sofa are vintage, millwork by Bill Truitt Woodworks (with finishes by Tony Montognese), and the walnut flooring is by Richard Marshall Fine Flooring.

Decker and Roddick were no strangers to home renovation, but as evidenced just from their first walkthrough, this latest undertaking would be on a scale they had not yet explored. The home had been little touched since its construction in 1964, and the couple would be only the second owners. Aside from obvious fixes like leaking ceilings and sagging floors, the layout, which was chopped up into a warren of tight quarters, needed a full gut to allow the space to breathe and gain more light. “We were parents of two young kids,” Decker says. “So the question was, How do we respect the grandeur of the house but also make it feel hospitable to a young family and one that can live up to the demands of everyday life?”

The dining room shows off many of the home’s thematic colors, including red, yellow, and green. Drapery fabric by Kravet, the pink chairs are vintage Kerstin Hörlin Holmquist, dining chairs by Studio Valle de Valle, antique farm table sourced from Obsolete, painting by Tyler Buck Guinn, and the pendants are by Of Enso, made with a vintage silk gingham from Decker’s personal collection.

The first-floor front room continues the nature theme thanks to its hand-painted custom mural. The sofa is a vintage Carl Malmsten upholstered in a Rose Uniacke fabric; the blue club chairs are vintage and sourced from Eneby Home; the leather chair is a vintage Hans Wegner; coffee table designed by Decker and fabricated by Dunham and Ernsberger Custom Cabinetry; and the armoire is a vintage walnut wet bar sourced from 1stDibs.

The kitchen hall’s allover paneling was fabricated by Bill Woodworks and installed by Blockhaus. Flush mounts by The Urban Electric Co.; the painting is a vintage William Skilling; sideboard by Bicyclette; and the rug is vintage found on Etsy.

The kitchen is painted in a muted shade of Decker’s favorite color: green. The double islands were designed by Decker and Dunham and fabricated by Ernsberger Custom Cabinetry; the pendants are by Roman and Williams Guild; the fittings by Waterworks; and the painting is an antique signed by Adelaide Briggs.

The breakfast nook brings the garden inside with its collection of plants and green accents. The table was custom-designed by Decker and Dunham and fabricated by Ernsberger Custom Cabinetry. The chairs are by Studio Ashby and upholstered with a Lee Jofa fabric, and the light fixture is a vintage Hans-Agne Jackobsson.

To help with the transformation, the couple engaged both Ruard Veltman Architecture for the architectural design and Stanwick Dunham for contracting. The group transformed the nearly 7,000-square-foot structure into a home that celebrates its lineage without being mired in the past. Nowhere is this effort more evident than in the gracious entryway, whose original carpeted staircase curved up from stark black and white tiles. And while that design wasn’t in poor taste, its severity read as both formal and cold. The solution was twofold: both to square-off the staircase and to clad the entire area in rich walnut paneling. The result not only allows sunlight to flow down from the second story, but showcases warm millwork. “We wanted it to look like it predated our arrival, and also be a bit more humble in its materials,” Decker says.

The primary bedroom’s wood floors and cream walls are softened up with the addition of a full wall of drapery, with fabric from William Morris. The chandelier is a vintage Carlo Scarpa sourced from 1stDibs, the bed from The Expert, linens from Nordic Knots, chair by Commune for George Smith, and the painting is by Alexandra Valenti.

Another view of the bedroom spotlights the family’s dog finding his light. Art by Tyler Hays Studio, nightstands by BDDW, vintage daybed from 1stDibs, and the vintage chair is sourced from Evan Reid.

The couple’s closet displays shoes almost in a museum-like setting, inside an antique French shoe cabinet sourced from 1stDibs. Ottoman from John Derian, the paint color is Farrow & Ball White Tie, and the chandelier is from RH.

The home’s primary bath was completely gut-renovated, but Decker wanted the design to appear original to the house. Tile from Waterworks, tub from Water Monopoly, side table by BDDW, painting by George Buckner of The Florida Highwaymen, and the pendant is an antique French copper lantern sourced from 1stDibs.

For the home’s interior design, Decker had no need of hiring a professional: She’s become a decorator herself. Over the last six or so years and mostly by word of mouth, the actor has spearheaded a variety of design projects (her latest, along with her design partners at By Idiots, being the interiors of Intown Golf Club’s new properties in Houston and Raleigh). For her family home, the brief was to keep the Georgian influence while updating the aesthetic. And it remains an evolving one: “Whenever I see that furniture dolly out, I know I’ll be involved at some point,” Roddick says.

Decker achieved the cozy yet elevated mix through color, using muted shades of green (her color), red, blue, and yellow; wallpaper with natural images like leaves or rivers; and plenty of vintage patterned rugs to soften up the wood floors. “It was originally old English meets early Georgian meets Shaker,” she says. “But when our kids became older, we really wanted to incorporate and take seriously what they wanted. Because, how cool to be eight and actually have some say in the space around you? So now the house is a hodgepodge of explosive color, a lot of which is totally inspired and dictated by them.”

The children’s playroom has a vintage feel while still being cozy. Sofa by RH, mohair chair and ottoman by Sam Klemick, wallpaper by Charles Voysey, and the shades are Fabricut fabric.

The couple’s daughter wanted her new room to match her softball team’s colors of red, white, and blue. Bed designed by Decker and fabricated by Liven UP, vintage chandelier sourced from PRB Collection, drapes from Anthropologie, and the rug is sourced from Hall Pass Vintage.

Decker’s office adds a bit of whimsy with a ceiling papered in a Pierre Frey design. Rug by Studio MRS for Nordic Knots, sofa by Coley Home, the desk is vintage, and the chandelier is by Apparatus.

An upstairs landing is one of Decker’s favorite places to snuggle with the family pets. Pendant by Roman and Williams Guild, dresser by Orior, the chairs are vintage Paolo Buffa upholstered in a Rose Uniacke fabric, table is vintage sourced from PRB Collection, and the pillows were made by Chancery Custom with vintage tapestry fabric sourced by Decker.

#5007. Amber Igiede Needs a Comeback. Good Thing She’s Built For It

The LOVB volleyball pro is sharing her ACL recovery journey in a new video series.

Amber Igiede was at the top of her game. The 25-year-old professional volleyball player had an illustrious college career at the University of Hawaii where she was a two-time All-American. After college, she signed a contract with League One Volleyball, where the middle blocker became one the faces of her team, LOVB Houston.

Now, winning games and breaking records have taken a back seat. Igiede’s focus is recovery.

This spring, Igiede suffered an intense ACL injury that will keep her off the court for the rest of the year. Healing her body—and staging an epic comeback—are her number one priorities.

Women’s Health can exclusively reveal that Igiede and her journey back to volleyball will be featured in Built for the Comeback, a LOVB-original series. The first episode is available now, and it features the athlete through the preliminary, intimate moments of recovery.

“I got really emotional watching it for the first time,” she tells WH. “It’s one of those things I’m savoring.”

Among the multitude of lessons Igiede has learned throughout this process, a principal one has been how to view herself as a person, not just an athlete.

“Anyone that really, truly goes through this knows how misleading the persona of an athlete can be when we’re going through something like this,” she says. “We are taught to ‘fake it until you make it’ and grind through everything.”

It takes Igiede back to when the COVID-19 pandemic hit while she was playing at Hawaii, and the wake-up call that came from a forced break from the sport. Now, she’s relying on the lessons she learned then to get her through this stage of her life and career.

“Every athlete knows that you dedicated so many years to this sport, so it’s a part of you,” she says. “When that part is taken away, there is sort of a grief process, and it’s very much magnified in the beginning.”

With her schedule considerably more open, Igiede says she has been able to explore new hobbies and find new outlets for joy. She says she has rediscovered her love for cooking and has been able to invest more time in her family and loved ones.

One of the best pieces of advice she received throughout her recovery process is to accept what happened to her, feel bad for herself a little, and then move on.

“You can’t spend too much time wallowing in what has happened, because you still need to look forward,” she says.

Her main focus right now is feeling strong. As a middle blocker, leg strength is crucial for Igiede to have the vertical she needs for the position. The main way she stays locked in on her goals to get her strength back is to physically write them down. She says this is how she beats her biggest competitor—herself.

For her specific injury, the recovery process is long. Because it was a complex, multi-ligament tear, the standard recuperation time is around 9-12 months. Igiede’s plan has been extremely methodical, relying on benchmarks to indicate when is the right time to incorporate something new to her regime.

Above all, she still remains grateful for the support from the league and her loved ones.

“It’s always such a privilege to play in the United States,” she says. “I played for the inaugural season [of LOVB], and I’ve always been super grateful that I’m able to play in this league. The opportunities they’ve given me, especially since this injury, they’ve helped so much.”

Looking ahead, Igiede isn’t just hoping to return to the player she was. She wants to come back even better, she says. “Every day is really an opportunity to get better and get back to where you were, or get back to where I can be even better than I was.”

Alyssa Cruz is the social media editor at Women’s Health, where she drives social strategy and helps shape the brand’s voice across platforms. Prior to WH, she worked at CBS News and palabra. #5006. Binance taps half its SAFU Bitcoin holdings, releases reserve proof

Binance’s SAFU Bitcoin wallet now holds about 7,500 BTC after a 7,499 BTC transfer linked to the hack, with no timeline for restoring the $1 billion fund.

Binance’s publicly disclosed emergency Bitcoin wallet held roughly half its previous balance on Monday after the exchange tapped its user protection fund to cover losses from Thursday’s $6.3 billion hack.

The exchange confirmed a transfer of 7,499 Bitcoin (BTC) on Saturday, linking it to the partial deployment of its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU).

As of Monday, the wallet held about 7,500 BTC, worth $583 million, down from about 15,000 BTC before the transfer.

The theft, the largest in cryptocurrency history, forced Binance to suspend withdrawals while it worked to replace the stolen assets. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korea on Saturday, identifying the hackers as TraderTraitor.

Binance began reopening withdrawals in phases on Sunday and said it had replenished approximately 95% of the affected assets, up from 90% a day earlier. It continued buying the remaining, less-liquid tokens through market and over-the-counter transactions.

The exchange is using its corporate treasury, SAFU and part of its futures insurance fund to cover the losses.

Binance’s SAFU policy outlines regular monitoring and rebalancing of the fund’s market value.

“If the fund’s market value falls below US $800 million due to BTC price fluctuations, Binance will rebalance the fund to restore its value to $1 billion,” it states.

Related: Binance hackers begin swapping stolen Solana tokens for Bitcoin: Chainalysis

The policy does not specify a timeline for replenishing funds withdrawn following a security incident.

Binance did not immediately respond to Cointelegraph’s questions about SAFU’s remaining reserves, further deployments and plans to replenish the fund.

Binance said Monday that users could now verify their balances against its Saturday proof-of-reserves snapshot after it completed the accompanying cryptographic proof.

The exchange said the snapshot showed customer holdings in 10 cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ether and USDT, were backed at least 1:1.

The exchange plans to take another snapshot covering more tokens on Wednesday, with the accompanying proof expected to take another 40 to 50 hours to generate.

#5005. The 10 Best Hiking Backpacks, Tested by Outdoor Gear Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

We tested dozens of packs and found Osprey’s Kestrel LT 45 to be the best.

A GOOD HIKING backpack is just as important—if not more so—as a good pair of hiking boots, hiking shoes, or any other hiking gear. Whether you're venturing deep into the backcountry or exploring a local trail, your pack will be strapped to your back for an extended period of time. It needs to be reliable, comfortable, durable, and offer the right storage and organization options to suit your style of hiking. Oh, and affordability is a nice-to-have, too.

Finding the right backpack for you can be like shopping for the perfect mattress. Backpack technology isn't what it used to be when your grandpappy was hitting the trail. It's far better but also a lot more complicated. You'll need to understand frame types and nylon fabric densities and hydration system compatibilities and—well, you get the picture. It's all just a little more confusing than it needs to be. That's why our expert team put together this guide to the best hiking backpacks to help you find the perfect pack without breaking your back and the bank in the process.

As an outdoors writer, I spend countless weeks outside each year. During that time, I've put the most popular and well-reviewed hiking backpacks to the test to determine the best of the best. Over the last 12 months, I've tested dozens of packs from Mystery Ranch, Gossamer Gear, Gregory, Osprey, and more throughout the U.S., in Utah's national parks, the White Mountains of New Hampshire, the vast deserts of Big Bend National Park, and beyond. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and some of his own personal testing. While testing hiking backpacks, I've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, ease of packing, weight, durability, how well (or not) the weight is spread throughout, and how much gear can fit in them.

So, whether you're looking for a featherweight daypack for afternoon peak-bagging or a full-fledged expedition pack for tackling the wilds of Patagonia, we've got you covered with the 10 best hiking backpacks for any trail.

Winner of this year’s “Best New All-Purpose Backpack” in the latest Men’s Health Outdoor Awards, the Kestrel LT 45 is the bag to buy if you only want to buy one. It’s Osprey’s reimagining of the classic rucksack design. It’s rugged yet lightweight, with a 45-liter capacity that’s more than enough for most hikers on all but the longest multiday treks. I personally love the streamlined exterior that cinches down tight for maximum compression. Osprey’s AirScape back panel offers just-right cushioning, coupled with simple torso-length adjustability to fit a wide range of body shapes and sizes.

After months of testing, this has consistently proven to be my go-to pack for most hikes because everything about it just works. Plus, the price point hits the midrange sweet spot, ensuring it’s affordable enough for most, even for first-time hiking backpack buyers on a budget. Bonus: An attached rain cover is included.

At just 12 liters and weighing only 390 grams, this pack is designed for ultra-efficient climbs and lightning-fast summit assaults. It's the daypack you grab when most other daypacks are too much. I found the simple organizational layout—one main compartment and two zippered pockets (one internal, one external)—made wrangling my day hiking essentials a breeze. Additional gear loops at the rear provide extra space for hanging anything you might need at the ready. The just-right back padding, removable hip belt, and ventilated mesh shoulder straps were extremely comfy for tackling daily summits in the White Mountains.

It's all made from recycled, eco-friendly materials that are Bluesign certified, with a PFC-free DWR treatment. The best part? It's among the most affordable brand-name speedpacks we'd recommend this year.

Like every Gregory pack I've tested in the last two decades, the Paragon 60 is durable, cleverly designed, and features smart organizational options. But I'm including it here mainly because it's so dang comfy to wear. It features a widely adjustable torso length and an airy mesh back panel that breathes well thanks to a design that's 90 percent air. The hip belt is equally adjustable, too, with dynamic panels that move independently of the frame. Translation: It's the most comfortable pack I tested this year, even after hundreds of miles of hiking with fairly heavy loads.

Bonus: The PFAS-free durable water-repellent (DWR) coating on the body, bottom, and pack lining means it's more eco-friendly, too.

Yeti’s first foray into the hardcore hiking backpack game comes on the heels of its recent acquisition of the Mystery Ranch brand. The Skala is a deft combination of Mystery Ranch’s legendary design prowess and Yeti’s built-to-survive-anything durability. The former’s RipZip opening is the star of this pack, providing instant access to its contents with a quick one-handed pull. The Skala features multiple adjustment points and a clever load distribution system that combine to ensure a perfect fit and all-day comfort on the trail.

True to the Yeti brand, it's packed with premium, heavy-duty materials built to survive years of abuse. The only downsides? At 3.4 pounds, it’s heavier than many in this weight class. It’s also pricier than most of its competition. But if you’re a fan of Yeti and/or MR and don’t mind the “buy once, cry once” price point, this is definitely worth considering.

For an all-in-one solution—a backpack that moves effortlessly from your morning commute to the office to the trail and back again—Peak Design's new Outdoor 25L pack delivers. The frameless, low-profile build is extremely comfy on and off the trail. The brand's signature organizational elements are here, too—it's hydration system-compatible, features a 16-inch laptop sleeve, and is purpose-built to accept PD's own gear cubes (sold separately) so you can divvy up the main compartment however you see fit. The drawstring/roll-top closure provides quick and easy access to the internal compartment while protecting your gear from the elements. Fair warning, though: You'll pay a premium for the PD brand name. If you’re looking to size up, the Outdoor Backpack is also available as a more generous 45-liter option.

Mountain Hardwear is upending the ultralight backpacking game with the debut of the all-new Alakazam series. The 45-liter model won a coveted spot in this year’s Men’s Health Outdoor Awards. At just 820 grams, it’s absurdly lightweight with a trail-friendly fit that feels like wearing nothing at all. Yet, it offers enough room for both gear-heavy day hikes and overnights. It’s all thanks to the bleeding-edge ALUULA shell fabric, which is not only light but extremely durable. The storage and organization (with plenty of loops, pockets, and oversized stash pouches) are cleverly laid out, and the unique GiddyUp compression system allows you to cinch your load down on the go. I also especially love the roll-top design that makes the entire bag waterproof. (A 60-liter option is also available.)

Like many Arc'teryx packs, the Alpha FL30 is first and foremost built for climbing (including a top strap, six lash points, and a built-in RECCO reflector for SAR situations). But, I also found its sleek silhouette and featherweight construction great for fast-packing. It's only as heavy as it needs to be while still protecting your gear with the brand's own abrasion-resistant Hadron grid fabric. The drawstring opening provides quick access to a cavernous, open-concept interior with only a single, small zippered security pocket.

It's a no-frills design with minimal organization options that won't please every hiker. But it's a solid, if pricey, option for hard-charging trail lovers who appreciate a pack that stays out of its own way.

With a 44-liter capacity, the Talon 44 is large enough for two-day weekender trips and even longer multiday treks. It's an ideal bag for most hikers looking to buy just one backpack that does it all. I love the slim profile, excellent padding, and close-to-body fit—all of which makes for more comfortable wear, especially after long days on the trail.

This iteration of Osprey's best-seller features a long list of upgrades to the straps, padding, and overall design. Plus, I found the sheer number of storage options to be perfect for almost any length of trip.

I’ve been a fan of Gossamer Gear’s featherweight fastpacker-friendly gear for years. The Grit 28 is my go-to for fast day hikes and quick summit assaults where I’m willing to trade comfort and convenience for speed. At just over a pound, the 28-liter pack is streamlined and sized right. The storage options are limited, ensuring you pack only what you need and nothing more.

What sets it apart from most of its competition is the vest-style shoulder and sternum straps that wear more like a racing vest for maximum all-day comfort. Despite its light weight, it’s made from two ultra-durable fabrics that I’ve found stand up to plenty of trail abuse.

The Crossroads 27L Carry-On is, first and foremost, a travel backpack (it fits under most airline seats, making it a great carry-on backpack). But Yeti bakes in plenty of trail-ready durability to make this one good enough for hiking, too. The 700-denier TuffSkin Nylon exterior is both water- and abrasion-resistant, with an extra durable and easy-to-clean PU-coated base. Contoured, EVA-foam shoulder straps and a no-pressure back panel make for easy carrying, even during long layovers.

Plus, with a suspended laptop sleeve and multiple zippered pockets inside and out, this has become my go-to weekender bag, especially on trips where I'm intent on hitting the trail straight from the airport. (Pro tip: Pair it with Yeti's own Crossroads packing cubes for maximum organization options.)

Ultimately, every hiking backpack is designed for hauling "stuff." The amount of stuff each pack can carry—its capacity—is measured in liters (L) or cubic inches. The right size for you depends on how long you typically hike for (hours, days, weeks?) and how heavy a packer you are. If you're shopping for your first pack, finding the perfect capacity can involve a little trial and error. But for a wide variety of hikers, the following numbers are a good starting point.

If you tend to pack light, the right capacity for you may fall closer to the lower end of the above ranges. If you're an over-packer (no shame!), consider sizing up to a slightly larger pack with a capacity on the upper end of the above ranges. Again: Trial and error.

You may have heard an old hiker's adage that goes something like, "Ounces make pounds, and pounds make pain." It's a simple axiom, but it's true: The more weight you carry, the more work you need to do on the trail. That's why it's important to pack as light as possible while still taking all the essentials. It helps to start with as light a hiking backpack as you can afford. The difference between three pounds and four pounds might not seem like much when you're standing in your living room, but I promise you'll feel every gram of that one-pound difference after 10 miles.

There are three main types of backpack construction: internal frame, external frame, and frameless. External frame packs have largely been phased out in the mainstream outdoor gear space in favor of internal frame models. True to the name, they feature a rigid structure that's "hidden" inside the pack's back panel. They sit closer to the back, hugging the body for a more streamlined fit that's ultimately more comfortable. All but the smallest hiking backpacks we recommend below rely on an internal frame construction.

Some compact daypacks (usually 20 liters or less) use a frameless construction similar to standard school backpacks. The lack of a frame means they're not ideal for supporting heavier loads, but that typically isn't an issue if you're only carrying enough for an afternoon hike. Without a frame, most of these packs collapse down almost completely flat, making them perfect travel backpacks.

Some packs—particularly those designed for alpine climbers—rely on top-loading-only designs. Think of a typical shopping bag where the contents are only accessible directly through the top opening. It's simple but limiting. Thankfully, many of the best hiking backpacks these days are accessible via both top and side openings. For larger packs, this makes it infinitely easier to get to the gear at the bottom of your pack without having to take everything out first.

The "best" storage layout is personal to each hiker. If you're an organizational nerd (I count myself among this camp), you may prefer more pockets to better wrangle your gear in a way that makes sense to you. On the other end of the spectrum are alpine-style bags that typically trade more pockets (and zippers and stitching) for a simpler, lighter-weight design. These tend to feature a single open-concept storage compartment with only one or two smaller storage pockets.

A few pieces of gear you want to pack in your hiking backpack include: a hydration bladder, water bottle(s), a phone (with easy access to its camera), a satellite messenger, and bear spray. Most modern bags also offer external storage options, like reinforced crampon patches and gear loops or "daisy chains" (i.e., webbing stitched into the pack's exterior that provides multiple attachment points for wet gear, ice axes, helmets, and more that you may not want to store inside your pack).

Modern hiking backpacks can be deceptively complex, and there are dozens of technical features available on many of today's best models. If you're shopping for anything other than a daypack, consider a bag with a dedicated sleeping bag compartment and sleeping pad straps. For longer treks where you may want to venture away from base camp once you set up your tent, a removable daypack (sometimes the "brain" or top lid of a larger pack converts into an ultra-compact hip bag for this purpose), and a rain cover, which may be a stand-alone piece of fabric with a stretch seam or sewn into the pack itself, so you can easily pull it over the pack if the weather turns south.

Mike Richard has traveled the world since 2008. He's kayaked in Antarctica, tracked endangered African wild dogs in South Africa, and survived a near-miss great white shark attack in Mexico. His travel advice has appeared on the websites for Forbes, Travel + Leisure, CNET, and National Geographic. He loves the great outdoors and good bourbon, and (usually) calls Tulsa, Oklahoma home. Mike also enjoys speaking in the third person.

He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. He holds a B.A. in Sport Management and is a Certified Beer Server, having previously covered the craft beer industry. Ryan currently lives on the water in New Jersey with his wife and their dog.

#5004. AI agent disputes head to ‘Internet Court’ — and a jury of AI agents

Who better to judge a dispute between AI agents than a jury of different AI models? That’s the idea behind GenLayer, which is already issuing thousands of judgements each day.

The world is headed towards a future in which AI agents will trade stocks and crypto, shop for your family, and much more. But what happens when a bot misinterprets an instruction to buy $10K of “blue chip stocks” and instead buys $10K of Bluebird-brand frozen chips?

Low-level agent disputes like this aren’t suited to the expensive and time-consuming existing legal system. Enter Internet Court, a new protocol that enables agents and humans to enter into contracts, with funds kept in escrow until the terms are judged to have been met.

The dispute resolution mechanism baked into the process employs GenLayer, an open, delegated proof-of-stake network of validators hooked up to AI models.

Operating in beta for the past year, it currently processes around 12,000 decisions per day. It authenticates user-uploaded photos for Collective Memory and resolves arguments on argue.fun. Mainnet is expected to launch next month.

The concept is a modern spin on the famous jury theorem proposed by philosopher Nicolas de Condorcet who argued the probability of reaching the correct answers increases as the number of independent evaluators grows.For Internet Court that means setting up a jury of AI agents from various models in the Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek families, along with a range of others.

“It’s not making the decision by using a single AI that would have some biases,” explains co-founder and CEO of GenLayer Albert Castellana. “It’s actually using a lot of different AIs, up to 1,500 different AIs. And when that happens, you have essentially better responses.”

“One is left-leaning, the other one is right-leaning. That’s how you get a better answer because one cancels the other.”

Disputes are resolved by sending the details to a randomly selected jury of five GenLayer validators, all running a different AI model. An initial decision is reached within minutes and is based on a simple majority vote, but the decision can be appealed to a wider jury of 11 agents, and then 23, and more and more until you hit the system’s limit.Castellana says finality typically occurs within 30 minutes. “If you wait until maximum finality, it is escalating rounds of appeal. You start with five, and it escalates to fifteen hundred, which could be three hours.”

The Court has 35 members in its open consortium so far, including well-known crypto firms such as ZKsync, NEAR, Consensys and UMA — which resolves disputes for Polymarket.

GenLayer has been in development for almost four years, and began life as an attempt to come up with a better way to evaluate what information is worthy of inclusion in an online knowledge base like Wikipedia.

In theory, anyone is supposed to be able to correct mistakes in the online encyclopedia but in practice, controversial topics from crypto to the war in Gaza get locked, with a small group of powerful editors getting the final say on contested information.

“The original idea behind GenLayer came with […] how could we have a decentralized Wikipedia?” he explains.

Related: Your fridge could one day stake Ether, launch memecoins — CFTC chair

GenLayer enables a new form of smart contract dubbed an “intelligent contract” that allows for subjective judgment. For example, you could contract a freelance writer and allow the system to automatically judge if their content is any good before paying them.

“We have a platform doing exactly this — paying influencers to write content online and then getting the money out,” he explains.

“Intelligent contracts can do code. They can do natural language. They can go to the internet. They can understand an image. They can have judgment,” he says.

The extent to which you can rely on an AI’s judgment in 2026 is limited by the capabilities of the technology. A standup comedian probably wouldn’t hire a joke writer via an intelligent contract.

Castellana explains the tech is also not good enough — yet — to judge whether a picture is a deepfake, or to resolve a boundary dispute between neighbors based on photos. It will certainly give you an answer, but you shouldn’t rely on it just yet. But there are plenty of occasions where AI judgments are already good enough. GenLayer automatically assesses photos uploaded by users to reality mapping platform Collective Memory for quality and accuracy and decides on a payment.

The other big user is Argue.fun, which enables users to bet on the resolution of arguments that are settled by lengthy debates between agents. The top four users have earned more than $2 million each. Most of the questions to date relate to serious policy issues around GenLayer governance, DAOs and AI safety.

Within the next few years, Castellana sees this process paving the way for genuinely autonomous DAOs that can automatically assess proposals according to the DAO’s constitution and wider aims.

GenLayer launches mainnet next month. Source: GenLayer

A more near-term use case is to resolve prediction market disputes more quickly. In mid-2025, Polymarket was sent into a spin over an ambiguously worded $240 million market on whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky would wear a suit before July. When he turned up at the June NATO summit wearing an outfit that was vaguely suit-like, the market initially resolved to “Yes.” But after nine days of appeals and back and forth among UMA token holder voters, the decision flipped to “No.”Castellana says GenLayer could shorten that period considerably.”It’s going to be resolved in a matter of minutes, and you will have hundreds, or thousands of AIs that make that vote very, very quickly. So at the end of the day, what you want is a neutral adjudication layer. You want something that is fast, accessible, and cheap.”

Whether humans will accept the decisions is another question entirely. But Internet Court and GenLayer aren’t designed to provide the final judgment, and decisions can still be appealed to humans.”After that, if you are still disagreeing and still think that Zelensky is not wearing a suit, what you can do is basically take it to Kleros, UMA, or even to a human court.”

Outsourcing dispute resolution to AI models comes with some big risks. The first is that the technology is just too immature to produce reliable judgments.

Another problem is that AI models reproduce many of the biases they find in the training data — and to date, the tech firms’ attempts to redress those biases have sometimes just flipped the bias in the other direction.

A third potential issue is a phenomenon described in an MIT paper called Representational Convergence. The paper suggests that over time, AI models from different companies all start to converge onto a similar statistical model of reality. If that’s true, then in five years Internet Court’s AI jurors could end up with a severe case of groupthink.

Castellana is not convinced this theory is valid. “I see many more models existing rather than fewer,” he says. “I see endless models coming from every country, every company, and every team. I cannot imagine that all of them will just converge into the exact same thing.”

#5003. What We Really Talk About When We Talk About Frivolous Things

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

There’s a scene in the 1996 film Trainspotting, based on the Irvine Welsh novel, and recently resurrected in London’s West End, where the boys ask the girls what they’re talking about, and the girls say, “Shopping!” Their throwaway response is shorthand for “frivolous girly things.” I enjoy conversations, with female friends and Gen Z clients alike, about “frivolous girly things”, except, in therapy, as in Trainspotting, we’re often talking about something deeper as well.

In my early career I had an 18-year-old client called Polly*. She was attractive and always immaculately made-up and fashionably dressed, with fantastic hair. She loved shopping for clothes and would often tell me about her latest buys. Most weeks, Polly complimented something about my appearance:

Polly was socially polite, compliant and genial. I liked her, and I liked talking with her about clothes and hair and make-up. We also talked about Polly’s strong need to be “likeable” and her self-identification as a “people pleaser”. She was exceptionally observant, hypervigilant at times, and we explored the ways this linked to her history of trauma.

But Polly noticed me too. With the benefit of hindsight (and experience), I understand Polly’s compliments as communicating something about our relationship that I’d missed an opportunity to explore. She noticed that I bothered to tidy up my hair and think about my clothes before I met with her, which demonstrated that I thought she was worth making the effort for. Her comments could therefore be interpreted as gratitude: “Thanks for caring.” I knew from the stories she shared that not everyone paid her the same level of respect, which was demonstrated in the ways they presented themselves when they met her.

Polly talked about the time she met her mother for coffee. Her mother, was shabbily clad in a tracksuit and trainers but had a dress and sandals in her bag to change into before she went on to lunch with “the girls”. The underlying message was: “You’re not important enough to make an effort for.”

Polly mentioned a tutor who showed her the jacket she’d purchased at lunchtime and quipped that it was much too nice to wear in college. In other words, “It’s much too nice to wear here, with you.”

And I’d heard about the boyfriend who refused to dress up for date nights but had no qualms about doing so for drinks with the boys. The unconscious communication was, “I’m bothered about them more than I’m bothered about you.”

Appearances mattered to Polly; it was a way to express herself and one of the few things she could control. But her compliments about my appearance communicated the importance of what it symbolised about our relationship too. The clues were there all along in what Polly shared with me about her other significant relationships, but I didn’t notice at the time.

So, when Polly complimented how I looked, it wasn’t about me, it was about us. Her unconscious communication was: “I’ve noticed you care about me and our relationship and I’m grateful.” I’ve learnt to be more curious about compliments and ever mindful of the subtleties of both my verbal responses and involuntary facial expressions. These are the unconscious communications that pass between my clients and me when we talk about frivolous girly things.

* Polly, her mother, her tutor and her boyfriend are fictitious composites.

#5002. 14 Best Airbnbs in the South of France for Bucolic Romance (2026)

The South of France has long been shorthand for bucolic romance. The region has drawn painters, film stars, and sun-starved travelers for generations, seducing them with endless vineyards and lavender fields, sleepy medieval villages, and its glittering Riviera. From Provence to the Côte d’Azur, the south of France offers a storybook mélange of rustic farmhouses, centuries-old castles and estates, along with honey-hued stone houses tucked into timeless hilltop towns.

Whether you fancy swimming in a pool besides your own château, late evening pétanque games at a centuries-old castle, gathering a group of friends at a hillside estate, or cozying up in a rustically romantic village apartment, Airbnb has options for turning every south of France fantasy into a reality. Here are some of the most extraordinary homes for rent in the region—spots so tempting, you might just want to cancel your return ticket and settle in for a year in Provence.

Perks: Mountain views, lake access, sauna, balcony, hot tub, indoor and outdoor fireplaces, pool table

While the South of France may be synonymous with summer, this contemporary chalet makes a compelling case for a winter escape with floor-to-ceiling windows that frame Sancy Valley’s mountain views. There’s plenty of room for up to 10 guests to spread out in this five bedroom home with a generous living space that includes three bathrooms and a pool table. Tucked in the hilly countryside, proximity to both Alpine and Nordic skiing is the property’s main draw for those looking to hit the slopes. After a day spent outside, both the indoor fireplace or sauna provide a perfect spot to warm up, though you could also enjoy the fresh air on the expansive balcony while keeping toasty by the outdoor fireplace or hot tub. From $1,048 per night.

Perks: Private backyard, fireplace, sound system, fully-equipped kitchen, security system, free parking, cleaning available for a fee

Located at the foot of Signal du Mailhebiau in the Aubrac region, this two-bedroom getaway is immersed in its rural landscape, surrounded by rolling fields, grazing cattle, and the French Countryside’s natural beauty. Originally built as a buron, or shepherd’s hut, the home has been thoughtfully transformed into a modern retreat that celebrates its architectural history. Hand-laid stone walls, vaulted ceilings, and a loft preserve the structure’s rustic character, while a dramatic wall of windows introduces a contemporary counterpoint, framing picturesque views of the expansive countryside. From $484 per night.

Perks: Private terrace, outdoor dining area, free parking, breakfast baskets delivered by request

Once the orangery of a stately chateau, this converted studio apartment retains its romantic design with soaring ceilings, a wall of French doors, and cheerful green-and-white checkerboard floor. Today, the space is an elegant retreat for two (or a couple with a baby thanks to the available crib), whether you’re spending leisurely afternoons indoors, sipping wine on the terrace, or exploring the surrounding vineyards and forests. For those looking to wander or partake in the region’s rich wine history, you’re about a 30-minute drive to the center of Bordeaux. From $165 per night.

Perks: Vineyard views, pool, outdoor shower, private backyard, fully-equipped kitchen, free parking, cleaning available for a fee

This isn’t so much a home to stay in as a castle to occupy. Situated on nearly ten acres of private parkland, this spacious 16th century château sleeps eight, while an additional two cottages can accommodate another eight guests. A large swimming pool, sun-drenched terrace, and lawn dotted with cypress trees practically beg you to throw a summer soirée. Inside, Château du Hameau’s historic bones remain prominent with original stone flooring, sweeping stairway, and ornate coiffured ceilings. With multiple fireplaces, soaking tubs, and seemingly endless views of fields and vineyards, this is a place to dream about long after you leave. From $1,825 per night.

Perks: Private tennis court, private pool, concierge service

Rustic architecture meets contemporary comfort at the sprawling Mas de l’Aiguebrun Estate, a super-sized stay with enough space to house up to 15 lucky guests. Old world design features like exposed brick and wood beam ceilings that date back to the 11th century contrast modern amenities like a La Cornue oven, waterfall showers, and even a mini rock climbing wall to entertain younger guests. The property has a prime location in Bonnieux, a village with an abundance of restaurants and cafes, as well as a Friday morning market that visitors swear by for local produce and baked goods. Back at the Airbnb, you’re encouraged to spend sunny days en plein air taking advantage of the picturesque outdoor amenities, which include an impressive stone-carved outdoor dining setup, 20-meter swimming pool, and a red clay tennis court to channel your inner Nadal. From $2,150 per night.

Perks: Private terrace, updated air conditioning, complimentary tea and coffee

Natural light floods this 16th century townhouse located in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, a village whose most famous residents include the likes of Pablo Picasso and Henri Matisse. Beautiful interiors are expected when your host is an interior designer, and this property delivers spatial excellence with considered details like a restrained color palette, layered textures, and contemporary furnishings. The combined kitchen and dining area is a perfect place to enjoy slow mornings (in fact, we think the envy-inducing pottery shelf is an idea you’ll want to recreate in your own space). A copper bath tub faces a king-sized bed in one of the main bedrooms, complete with a window view overlooking the surrounding foliage. For more private guests, the property also has three en suite bathrooms in a glassy green color palette, each housing their own tubs and showers. If you’re hoping to explore your charming provincial surroundings, lots of art and shopping attractions await; plus, the 40-minute drive to Nice makes it convenient to plan a day trip or two. From $649 per night.

Gilded light fixtures, muted textiles, and farmhouse furniture all distinguish this abundantly pastoral stay on the French Riviera. While there’s plenty of classic provincial charm to immerse yourself in—exposed wood beams, stone flooring, and two fireplaces—the design also ties in moments of splashy Mediterranean character with coastal furnishings and colorful tilework. It’s worth stopping by the local markets to gather ingredients for a meal or two in the fully-equipped kitchen, with its pine green cabinetry, Smeg stove and matching dishwasher, as well as a dishware collection rounded out by plenty of Serax ceramics for a festive dinner party. When you are looking to venture out, the surrounding Roquefort les Pins offers a small community of indie stores run by locals, and eateries, while more lively attractions in Nice, Antibes, and Cannes are just a 30 minute drive away. From $693 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, heated pool, pétanque court, chef, cleaners, and airport transfer available upon request, close to wineries and a golf course

This nine-bedroom complex sleeps a crowd, but no matter how many people you arrive with, you’re bound to be struck by the ultra-private feeling of the estate. The centuries-old stone buildings surrounded by cypress trees originally comprised a farm, but today have been converted into three buildings fit for at least 16 guests. Inside, the oversized rooms are filled with cushy leather couches, bentwood chairs, and cozy beds. Outdoors, the scenic grounds are just right for a heated game of pétanque or a dip in the heated pool. From $2,894 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, heated pool, air conditioning, indoor fireplace, crib, cleaning available during your stay, pizza oven

If you’ve been daydreaming of your very own French estate, it’s entirely possible you’ve manifested this Airbnb into being. Nestled in the Provençal countryside near the village of Gordes, the 12-bedroom home offers striking mountain views alongside a range of picturesque outdoor perks that include a heated pool, pétanque court, and an elegant garden. The home’s original features have been thoughtfully maintained, from the exposed stone walls to the vaulted ceilings, while the interiors lean into pastoral elegance with farmhouse furnishings and creamy linens. Not too far from the villa, you can traipse through the infamous lavender fields and vineyards that have become synonymous with the region. From $959 per night.

Perks: Ocean-front views, central AC, swimming pool, security system

This palatial estate on the French Riviera might be large enough for a royal wedding, but that doesn’t mean you can’t book the six-bedroom home all for yourself. Everything about this rental is over-the-top, from the palm trees that flank the front door to the grand entry hall complete with marble columns, a sweeping staircase, and ceiling frescos. Staying here feels a bit like having a castle all to yourself, one where you can while away the days outside in the gardens, by the pool, or along the nearby shores. The grand, high-ceilinged spaces interiors are outfitted with antique furnishings and chandeliers, along with an elective blend of mid-century pieces and lots of artwork. Should the mood strike for a soirée fit for a king, the home’s living room and conservatory can easily accommodate 200 for a cocktail party. From $10,350 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, extensive grounds, heated pool, cleaning available during your stay

For those “go big or go home” vacations, go ahead and book a grand castle. This one is from the 17th century and encompasses over 300 acres of forest, farmland, and vineyards. The property itself features nine bedrooms, most which have ensuite bathrooms with soaking tubs, terracotta and stone floors, exposed stone walls, and bright and airy rooms doused in bright colors like marigold to cerulean. Inside and out, there are multiple seating areas, including a music room and dedicated office, to gather with guests (accommodating over a dozen people at any given time). From $2,458 per night.

Perks: Sleeps a crowd, piano, washer and dryer, pool, EV charger, exercise equipment, pool and pink pong tables, outdoor dining area

This sprawling farmhouse just outside the village of Mouriès sleeps at least 16 people and has plenty of room, both inside and out, for everyone to sprawl out. The 10 bedrooms all come with en-suite bathrooms, and there are multiple living rooms for gathering in smaller groups—ones accented in antique tiles, marble fireplaces, vaulted stone ceilings, and sumptuous couches. The most striking room in the home is the dining room, with its geometrically wall mural, exposed antique wooden ceiling beams, and a table that seats 26. But this being the south of France, the outdoors is equally as beautiful, and you’ll find a large alfresco dining area, plenty of loungers, a pristine swimming pool, and grassy lawn. From $3,447 per night.

Perks: Long term stays available, washer and dryer, located in a walkable village

If you were to run a Google image search for the term “French provincial house,” this two-bedroom home might be the first one to populate the results. It doesn’t get more quintessentially French than this colorful home set within the village of Bormes les Mimosas. The whole space, from its colorful limewashed walls to its checkerboard kitchen, give off the feel of an artist’s retreat. And if a true retreat is what you’re looking for, feel free to linger a while (long-term stays are very welcome here). From $359 per night.

Perks: Within a walkable village, crib, highchair, and children’s toys available, pets allowed, fireplace, central AC
