#5001. Weighted Daggers. Sword Yoga. Real-Life Gauntlets. Welcome to the World of Romantasy-Inspired Fitness.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You’ll still break a sweat, but with “the added bonus of feeling badass.”

The female warrior lunges, her sword slashing in the sunlit forest. Clad in black armor, she spins, whirling her weapon over her head. Silver slices the air. She jumps, spins, then kicks. No, this isn’t a Valkyrie training scene from the newest installment in Sarah J. Maas’s hit romantasy (romantic fantasy) series, A Court of Splintered Harmony. It’s a workout class.

Charity LeBlanc didn’t set out to create a romantasy-inspired workout program. Originally, the former American Ninja Warrior semifinalist just wanted to share videos of her fitness journey and fantasy-inspired cosplay creations on social media—and her follower count grew. Then, in 2024, she heard about the Dragon Gauntlet, a Fourth Wing-inspired obstacle course race in Boyne Falls, Michigan. She asked her followers if they wanted to train together for the event, and designed a workout program that combined strength training, HIIT cardio, combat circuits, and weapons training. “It wasn't just working out to do a rep; it was to gain a skill,” says LeBlanc. “And it took off.”

Romantasy-inspired workout programs have exploded over the last few years, mirroring the genre’s takeover of the publishing industry. After reading A Court of Thorns and Roses in 2022, trainer Samantha Willens put her Harry Potter- and Star Wars-themed Pilates classes on pause and shifted her focus to workouts inspired by the bestselling romantasy series. She created the Valkyrie Squad Program, a four-month fitness plan based on the series’ fifth book, A Court of Silver Flames—and her business, Micro Squad, grew exponentially.

In 2024, Sabina Storberg launched WeaponUp, a sword yoga platform, thinking it would attract women into traditional martial arts or yoga. But “it was actually the book girls,” she says. Now, they have thousands of members around the world.

Sure, gaining the endurance of a dragon rider, the agility of a half-Fae assassin, or the muscle of a Valkyrie warrior (IYKYK!) isn’t your average fitness goal, but that’s why these workouts work. Romantasy books allow women to fall in love with stories of female empowerment—and these workouts allow women to live out those stories in real life. “There's something to be said for channeling a character you admire, especially one who embodies strength, confidence, and resilience,” says exercise physiologist Rachelle Reed, PhD. “For some women, that connection might make exercise feel more fun and approachable, or even help them feel more confident trying something new.”

Here’s how women are taking on their own version of a heroine’s journey—and what mixing sweat with a little bit of magic has done for their minds and bodies.

Jamie Dalton, 38, never really enjoyed working out, especially in front of other people. She always struggled with coordination, which made her self-conscious. “Weight training was the closest to me enjoying something because that required the least amount of coordination,” Dalton says. “But it just felt more like a punishment, and punishments, you don't keep doing long-term.” She’d often start a workout program only to stop a few months later.

But when Dalton discovered WeaponUp, her relationship with fitness transformed. The classes consist of sword drills and choreographed flows inspired by romantasy characters, like Nesta Archeron from ACOTAR and Manon Blackbeak from Throne of Glass. And while the workouts are rooted in fantasy, the moves are a real fusion of kung-fu and yoga, and involve a lot of squats, lunges, kicks, core work, balance, and mobility. They also present a mental challenge as you learn to wield a sword with each hand and on either side of the body. Five months in, and Dalton is still going strong with WeaponUp, training four to five times a week.

While working out wasn’t totally foreign to Dalton, many of the people who sign up for WeaponUp, Whimsy Forge, and Micro Squad are new to exercise. Romantasy-inspired fitness “lowers the barrier to entry” because it speaks to people’s existing interests and feels personalized; they can put themselves in the shoes of the strong female protagonist(s) they’ve admired in book form, Reed says.

For instance, all of Whimsy Forge’s eight-week workout plans, called character arcs, are designed to emulate a different fantasy character's abilities, whether that's an Elven Huntress’ agility, a Dragon Rider’s endurance, or a Valkyrie Warrior’s strength. Whichever workout plan you choose, you’ll still do classic exercise moves, such as squats and presses, as well as optional special skill challenges that require a (play) weapon. “I'm really passionate about making sure the programs are accessible, and I am not a gym girl,” says LeBlanc. “For a lot of the workouts, all you really need is a yoga mat and some space.”

Both the level of access and the genuine enthusiasm for the subject matter are enough to help some people get started with fitness, which is often the hardest part. “When people are new exercisers, if they have an enjoyable or interesting experience the first few times, it's easier for them to start building toward a habit,” says Reed. “Eventually, your discipline and intrinsic motivation pick up.”

Of course, romantasy-inspired fitness can also help more experienced exercisers get out of a workout rut. Brooke Lydon, 33, used to love taking fitness classes, but between a full-time job and raising her 4-year-old daughter, she didn’t have the time. A fan of yoga teacher Taylor Johnson, Lydon thought that doing her fantasy-inspired strength and mobility program, Arius, might be a fun way to get back into fitness, and she liked that she could do the program at home.

Plus, it gave Lydon an extra opportunity to listen to her romantasy audiobooks during workouts, which doubled as a form of motivation. She’d often imagine herself competing against her favorite characters and end up working harder. “I would be like, ‘If she can do it, I have to do it,’” she says.

Romantasy-inspired fitness may offer an extra incentive to exercise, but it’s also just plain fun. Each program infuses a sense of childlike joy and wonder into workouts. “We don't have that many fun fitness experiences available to us—everything is for a goal,” Storberg says. “I'm going to go to the gym so I gain muscle, and that's very important, but we don't make it fun like we used to when we were children.”

Can a romantasy workout provide the same level of results as traditional strength training or cardio? For Dalton, who was losing muscle and experiencing joint pain due to perimenopause, the answer is a resounding yes. “I definitely feel like I've regained some of the mobility that I felt like I was losing, and I've definitely regained a lot of the strength back,” she says.

WeaponUp classes have also helped Dalton improve her coordination, thanks to the focus on proprioception (the understanding of where your body is in space). “You're doing your whole flow on a yoga mat, and you might have your kids' stuff in one corner, so you have to have a really good understanding of where you are in space, where the sword is in space,” says Storberg.

But sword yoga also provides balance training in a more accessible way, especially since you have a prop. “When I try to do a squat normally, I feel like I'm going to fall over,” Dalton says. “But because of the flow that they have you do with a sword, somehow it counterbalances so I feel more grounded and secure.”

Meanwhile, in Micro Squad’s Pilates-based classes, you’ll do moves like Russian twist punches with (optional) Dragon’s Edge weighted daggers that evoke a character or pivotal scene from ACOTAR through the series called “A Fortnight in Prythian.” As such, you’ll experience many of the same muscle endurance benefits that come from any low-weight, high-rep workout. But there’s also “the added bonus of feeling badass while wielding weighted daggers and immersing yourself in the world,” Willens says.

Additionally, in the Valkyrie Squad program, you’ll train foundational strength and mobility skills before progressing to martial arts, kickboxing drills, and sword training, like the warrior characters in A Court of Silver Flames. Many Micro Squad members finish the program feeling not only confident in their bodies, but also like they can take on any obstacle—physical or mental, Willens says.

It’s no coincidence that a fitness program based in fantasy can lead to real-life gains. If you can build confidence with a class you find interesting, you’re more likely to stick with it for the long-term, Reed says. In fact, several WeaponUp members have lost 50 pounds or more after starting the program. “That got them into a trajectory of getting into wellness [and] being able to really take their health back,” Storberg adds. “There's so many women that are actually sticking to a fitness routine because it's fun, unique, and different.”

Badassery is the intangible benefit that all romantasy-themed workouts seem to share. “A lot of women have never seen themselves as this person who is strong, who is capable, who can do skills, but walking into these programs where they feel like they're becoming something, that transformation is real for them,” LeBlanc says. “They actually are becoming stronger.”

With the popularity of romantasy fitness only growing, it’s also evident that more women are invested in what their bodies can do, not what they look like. For as much as the average romantasy female main character may uphold traditional beauty standards, that’s not why millions of readers love them, or why thousands want to work out like them. “It's not just about getting a smaller waist or growing glutes. A lot of women's fitness is about how you look and less about how it makes you feel,” says LeBlanc. “[This is] a lot more motivating and empowering.”

Romantasy-inspired fitness has even helped Dalton navigate discussions with her 7-year-old daughter about exercise, food, and health in general. “It's made it a lot easier to turn that conversation into becoming strong and powerful, instead of skinny,” she says. Her daughter will often join her for WeaponUp workouts, and “that has been a really cool thing for me as a mom,” Dalton says. “I want my kid to exercise in a way that's going to help her build healthy habits, and I love that this is letting me do that with her.”

Fantasy fitness is becoming more than just a workout trend—it’s a way for fans to connect beyond the pages of their favorite books. Whimsy Forge hosts a semi-annual Trial of the Guilds, a community-wide virtual fitness challenge where members choose one of the aforementioned character arcs, and everyone in the same arc becomes a Guild, or team. Then, all the Guilds compete against each other for eight weeks. “We do it as a community, so you feel like you're with friends and people that are going to encourage you,” says LeBlanc.

In addition to online fitness programming, several of these platforms now offer in-person classes and meetups. The WeaponUp team just finished a 10-city Graceful Warrior tour that took them from coast to coast, attracting a range of ages, sizes, and fitness abilities, says Storberg: “What they have in common is this desire to be the main character.” That desire is so strong for Dalton that she’s willing to drive three or four hours to attend an in-person WeaponUp event. “[I’d] go and make a whole day of it,” she says.

The collective power of the book girls, both online and in-person, is not to be underestimated. “Having a community can provide accountability, encouragement, and a sense of belonging, which can all make it easier to stick with an exercise routine over time,” says Reed. “But what's particularly interesting here is that these women are connecting over more than just exercise. They already have a shared interest in the books, characters, and stories, which gives them another way to connect with one another.” (Perhaps unsurprisingly, Whimsy Forge, WeaponUp, and Micro Squad all boast virtual book clubs.)

While many women are initially drawn to romantasy fitness because of a connection to a character, they not only forge new connections with other readers, but ultimately, themselves. “It’s less about acting like some of these female main characters that we see in the books, but rather becoming a female main character in your own life,” says Storberg. After all, who needs a shadow daddy when you can swing a sword?

Lindsay Geller is the lifestyle director at Women’s Health, where she oversees the Sex & Love, Relationships, and Life sections. She has more than 10 years of experience covering sex, relationships, health, fitness, and general lifestyle topics for print and digital publications. She is also a NASM-certified personal trainer and lives in New Jersey with her husband, daughter, and rescue dog.

#5000. 7 Best Shaving Creams for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Expert

Say goodbye to razor burn and hello to a better shave.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

UNLESS YOU'RE SHAVING with a top-notch wet or dry electric razor, you’ll need to first apply a product to prep the skin. There are really only two options: pre-shave oil and shaving cream. For the smoothest, most irritation-free shave, opt for both in order. However, the latter is a non-negotiable unless a red, sliced-up face is the look you’re going for. No judgment?

The truth is, your shave is only as good as the cream you use because the right shaving cream cushions the skin, reduces irritation, and locks in moisture for added comfort afterwards. It also helps the razor glide smoothly, preventing nicks and tugging.

Most importantly, it turns a tedious routine into a clean, refreshing experience. But not all shaving creams are created equal—some barely protect or soothe at all. To save your skin the abuse (and potential scars), I’ve rounded up the best options worth trying.

Jackfir The Classic checks every box I look for in a shaving cream. Its ingredients are clean, its scent soothing, and the formula protects the skin from irritation and cuts. Simply put, I got one of the closest, smoothest shaves I’ve ever had with this cream.

The creamy lather cushions the razor perfectly while aloe, cucumber, and panthenol keep the skin calm and hydrated. The scent is invigorating and woodsy, thanks to natural oils like cedarwood, vetiver, and chamomile instead of synthetic fragrances. This also makes it safe for sensitive skin without being entirely scentless.

On top of its long list of at least 70 percent organic ingredients, it even comes in sustainable packaging made from recycled materials. I generally shave with a safety razor for my face and a cartridge razor for my body (or when traveling), and Jackfir was perfect for both.

It’s slick enough that it never clogs up the blade, but thick enough to keep my skin protected. This is all on top of prepping the skin while also locking moisture in post-shave.

I have dry skin that’s prone to shaving irritation, but the combo of panthenol and bisabolol kept my face feeling calm before and after the session. You also don’t need to use much to cover your entire face; barely more than a nickel-sized amount will do the trick. The only downside to this stuff is that it’s over $35, but given how long it lasts and how great it performs, it’s well worth it.

The razor you use isn’t solely responsible for shaving irritation. For many, simply switching to a gentler, more skin-friendly shaving cream will go a long way in preventing bumps and redness. You won’t find a better option than Harry’s Shave Cream, which is no surprise coming from what I dubbed the best skincare brand for clean-shaven men.

This cream packs powerful natural ingredients like eucalyptus oil, mint oil, and aloe vera, which work together to soothe skin and reduce irritation. It’s free of parabens, sulfates, or other common irritants, and its formula is equally thick and silky to protect and smooth skin. Best of all, it could double as the best value shaving cream at only $8 a container.

I’ve been cutting my own hair for over a decade, so I really only go to barbershops for one thing: a close and luxurious shave. But this shaving cream makes me wonder if I could eliminate those trips altogether. It’s the closest you’ll get to the barbershop experience with an incredible, soft lather that feels like a hot towel wrapped around your chin. Sure, it’s a little pricey and best applied with a brush—which I count as a positive—but it’s far less expensive and time-consuming than making a trip to your local shop.

If you’re prone to razor bumps and burning like me, this cream will feel like a godsend thanks to its rich and smooth lather that’s packed with ingredients that care for skin. The aloe vera and shea butter deliver deep hydration, keeping your face calm and protected while helping to prevent razor bumps and irritation.

The pair also works together to calm inflammation, moisturize, and create a protective barrier that helps prevent razor bumps and post-shave irritation. White tea extract then adds that clean, refreshing feel I always look for in a shaving cream. It’s soothing, nourishing, and bump-free.

I don’t use cartridge razors too often, as safety and electric razors tend to leave my sensitive skin less irritated. But if I’m traveling or in a hurry, I’ll turn to them—and rarely without this shave gel from GilletteLabs. The rapid foaming is as advertised, thickening in seconds for quick application.

It gives that fresh feeling once it hits your face before the razor even touches your skin. While it’s listed as having a cedar wood and orange peel scent, I rarely catch too much of it. But I prefer that, as I’d rather rely on my cologne for fragrance.

I implore you to use a shave oil in addition to a cream to minimize irritation as much as possible; however, if you really don’t have the time or desire to, use this. Atwater’s shaving cream is designed to pull double duty, preparing the skin before the razor touches it and protecting it throughout the shave. As a pre-shave, its blend of hydrating oils helps soften stubble and create a smooth, conditioned surface.

During shaving, ingredients like vitamin B5, vitamin C, argan oil, and coconut oil work together to cushion the blade, reduce friction, and keep the skin nourished. This combination leaves my skin feeling as calm and moisturized as it’ll get without using a pre-shave oil. Plus, it’s completely unscented, so it’s safe for even the most sensitive skin.

Dr. Squatch’s shave butter feels more like a creamy lotion than shaving cream, allowing the razor to glide smoothly across the skin while it also moisturizes. Despite how that sounds, it never clogs up my blade—even when I use a safety razor. The trio of natural hero ingredients, shea butter, murumuru butter, and macadamia oil, is rich in vitamins and fatty acids that deeply hydrate, soften, and smooth the skin.

Together, they create a nourishing barrier that locks in moisture and helps reduce irritation for a more comfortable, soothing shave. The lotion-like texture takes a couple of shaves to get used to if you’ve traditionally used thicker shave creams or foams, but the feel of your skin during and after is immediately satisfying.

Shaving cream is often used as a catch-all term for several products that prep and protect your skin while you shave. There are three main types, and the right one depends on your razor, your skin type, and your personal preference.

If your shave is only as good as the cream you use, then the cream is only as good as its ingredients. Shaving creams often include soothing ingredients like aloe vera, which calms irritation and helps the skin stay hydrated before and after shaving. Shea butter is another popular one, as it provides rich moisture that softens hair and improves razor glide, reducing friction during the shave.

Many formulas also contain vitamin E, an antioxidant that nourishes the skin and supports repair after shaving. Then there is a slew of natural oils and other vitamins to keep an eye on, like vitamin B5, vitamin C, argan oil, and coconut oil that hydrate, soothe, and prevent post-shave irritation.

How often do you shave? That’s the most important question to ask yourself when considering the size of your cream. A larger tube offers better value and lasts longer, especially for daily shavers. Smaller sizes, on the other hand, are ideal for travel or testing a new formula before committing. You’ll also want to consider what you shave.

I rock a beard most of the time, so I only shave for touch-ups on my neck and cheeks. Plus, I rarely shave body hair and stick to trimming. Because of this, I can often get away with a smaller tube. But if you’re clean-cut or shave large parts of your body, you’ll want to look to larger options.

We’ve been testing razors since 2018, and naturally, every swipe meant testing the shaving creams that make them glide, too. For this update, I considered old favorites and new offerings from brands I trust to find the best-performing creams on the market. After over a year of testing (and plenty of shaves), I narrowed dozens down to 15 top contenders. I then evaluated or reevaluated each formula for cushion, glide, price, and how well it prevented irritation. After all that lathering, these seven shaving creams earned the title of best in 2026.

#4999. The Best Dining Room Lighting Ideas to Set Your Space Aglow

As romantic as candlelight dining sounds, it’s simply not practical (way too much wax!). The best dining room lighting ideas are thoughtfully planned: They take your actual eating habits, furniture proportions, room structure, and budget into consideration. They weigh the benefits of pendant lights vs. chandeliers vs. flush mounts and wall sconces, not to mention bulb type.

Lighting, it turns out, gets pretty involved—which is why we’ve tapped interior designers from around the country for their brightest ideas. And though the considerations are complex, modern lighting can be just as romantic as the candlelight option. “The evolving landscape is opening the door to more thoughtful layers and innovative ideas for how lighting can shape a space,” says Mike Shively of Chicago-based AD PRO firm En Masse Architecture and Design. “Lighting and coziness are both things we associate with luxury today, and neither necessarily comes down to price.”

In fashion designer Marysia Reeves’s Venice Beach home, a breezy, lantern-like fixture hovers above the wood dining table.

Pendant lighting gets more playful when each piece hangs at a different height. The look works especially well with a vaulted ceiling, as evidenced by this dining room set in a pavilion at the back of the house. “A cluster of glass pendants hung at staggered heights works alongside a pair of table lamps on the sideboard to create warm, layered light,” says Lucas Goldbach of En Masse Architecture and Design, who worked on the project.

The varying heights of the pendants gives this light fixture some dimension.

In this stunner of an LA home by design collective the Archers, a Le Corbusier–inspired table is lit with simple can overhead lights (definitely dimmable versions).

Lighting options are about more than just form. A more traditional shape can look entirely new when cast in a surprising material. “Our recommendation is to rethink conventional finishes and materials wherever possible,” says Sarah Goesling of Goesling Group, an AD PRO Directory firm based in Chicago. “For a chain-mail fixture, look beyond stainless steel to a striking yellow gold. For braided metal hardware, trade the ruggedness of wrought iron for the refined sheen of polished gunmetal.”

For a dining room in a midcentury-modern home, Goesling Group chose an appropriately retro 1950s-inspired Nabila chandelier by Tooy. And to add a modernized touch through the materials, they went with smoked glass around the bulbs.

A Sputnik-style fixture draws the eye up in this dining room by Goesling Group.

If you find an antique fixture you love, it might be worth rewiring the piece. Source on sites like eBay, Etsy, and 1stdibs, or take a lap around your local flea market. Alternatively, scour relatives’ attics and basements for a fixture with some family history. In the dining room below, designed by En Masse Architecture and Design, the light fixture was originally bought by the homeowner’s parents and was refurbished by Archistoric. “It became the inspiration for many of the metal finishes used throughout the new design,” says Goldbach.

This En Masse Architecture and Design dining space is crowned by an heirloom chandelier, refurbished by Archistoric.

Sconces, floor lamps, even table lamps can do the job of overhead pendant and flush-mount fixtures—so don’t force one if you’re not sure you like the look at all (proof, via Amélie Colombet’s apartment).

Fixtures made from natural alabaster stone are popular because of the warm, glare-free glow they emit. And because the translucent material has natural veining, no two pieces are alike. You can find alabaster in a variety of shapes—including linear forms, mini pendants, and semi-flush-mount ceiling lights—and while it’s generally pretty pricey (ranging anywhere from $300 for a single alabaster pendant lamp to $3,000 for a row of pendants), it’s also a durable material that lasts.

In the dining nook below, designed by Goesling Group, the minimal fixture makes a major impression. “It’s a solid alabaster stone piece lit all the way around the rim that looks like the moon when it glows,” says Goesling.

The pendant sets a striking tone in this cozy dining nook by Goesling Group.

If you have no interest in hardwiring a thing . . .Get an arc floor lampYou can have proper overhead lighting for your dining area without hardwiring a thing overhead. All you need is an arc floor lamp; they plug right into a wall outlet but stand tall, with a long, curved neck that will position the bulb and shade directly over your table. (How’s that for simplified?) The Arco floor lamp by Flos is a classic, but more budget-conscious shoppers can spring for similar styles from retailers like Wayfair (or even Amazon!).

If you’re trying to decide between options . . .Take the shape and style of your table into considerationThe overhead fixture you choose and the table itself “don’t have to [have] a direct geometrical correlation, but there should be some proportional consideration,” says Russell Groves of New York City–based Groves & Co. A long or unusually large chandelier would obviously overpower a short table, and vice versa: A teeny-tiny bulb might look silly above a big table. Same goes for the look: A lovely old farmhouse table would do well with a lovely farmhouse fixture or something super-modern for contrast—but either way, they should be considered together.

If you’d like to jazz up a fixture you already own . . .Customize the lampshadeA reflective material inside the shade will help cast light back down toward the table, Groves points out, while perforated shades will turn any bulb into a twinkly light (if that’s your prerogative). “Textured fabrics like raw silk will add a beautiful warmth and shadow to a room,” he says, but should you require a more directional cast, “an opaque shade wouldn’t give you a lot of glow in the room but would put more on the table.” Just because a fixture has shades you’re not into doesn’t mean it’s the end of the line. Swap them out!

If you’re sick of the typical dining room look . . .Consider less-traditional fixtures“Unreal times call for surreal styles, and lighting is emerging as a particularly compelling canvas for experimentation,” says Goesling. “From blown-glass designs with off-kilter stripes, to chain-mail, tapestry, and wrought iron reimagined through unexpected finishes and geometric patterns, these materials and techniques are taking on a new life. We anticipate seeing this influence extend across lighting, from woven metal sheaths and illustrative shades to sculptural, cast forms.”

A unique accent light sometimes even doubles as art. Such is the case in a Chicago penthouse designed by Kuchar, which features a dining room fixture with a strikingly sinuous form. “Going for the cool, funky light fixture has become the new normal among our residential clients,” says Sarah Kuchar-Parkinson, owner and creative director of the Chicago-based studio. “Not only does it bring brightness and light, but it adds architectural interest and an element of quirk.”

A statement-making light fixture hovers above the dining room table of this Kuchar-designed Chicago penthouse.

When hanging a pendant or a chandelier . . .Take care to hang it at the correct heightToo high and a pendant lamp might look stuck to the ceiling, constricted; too low and you won’t be able to see your guests around it. Somewhere in between is just right, so step back and consider it at various lengths before settling on one. “When you’re seated, you don’t want [the fixture] to be in your face—the same way everyone gets annoyed when flowers are in the way,” Groves says.

If you’re into geometric lines . . .Get creative with the cordWhen hanging a pendant lamp with a very simple silhouette, feel free to get creative with the cord: Zigzag it from wall to wall around a corner, tack it in swags along the ceiling, or loop it over a hook on the wall.

To soften overly bright overheads . . .Add a dimmerDesigner Sam Allen of Sam Allen Interiors, based in Weston, Connecticut, feels strongly about the worth of a dimmer switch: “If your dining room chandelier is not hooked up to a dimmer, call an electrician right now. I mean it. Don’t even finish reading this—call your electrician first.” With the simple pressing of a lever or turning of a knob, dimmable lighting allows you to control the brightness of the bulbs, which is particularly important if you’re dealing with often-harsh overhead lighting. “To me, chandeliers should mimic candlelight,” says Groves—and that warm, dim glow is possible if you just install dimmers. Plus, they’re available in both modern and traditional silhouettes that will add considerably more charm to the walls than those plastic switch plates you hate anyway.

To make the room multifunctional . . .Supplement the lighting solution you chooseIf you end up setting your table with some nice, warm candlelight, you might need to add sconces or downlights to supplement that glow when the room is used for anything other than an intimate dinner. (Dining room tables are very good for DIY projects, we’d like to note.) And to up a room’s cozy factor, lean into lamps. “The more lamps the better,” says Goldbach. “We like using smaller-scale lamps and vintage pieces in unexpected ways to create a warm, layered atmosphere. Multiple light sources can make the space feel cozier and more inviting, especially as the days get shorter.”

If you’re a fanatic about light quality . . .Be selective with the bulbsWarm white light, cool light, bright light—you can get exactly the brightness level you desire with the right bulb. For lots of ambience, try vintage-inspired filament bulbs. If it’s more of a particular shape and style you’re after for an exposed-bulb fixture, try decorative bulbs. And for the ultimate in energy efficiency, invest in LED bulbs, which are up to 90 percent more efficient than traditional light bulbs.

#4998. Strategy spends triple its weekly Bitcoin outlay on STRC buybacks

Strategy spent $208.2 million buying back STRC preferred shares and $65.5 million on Bitcoin, while allocating $98.5 million to its USD Cash balance.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy spent more than three times as much buying back its STRC preferred shares as it did acquiring Bitcoin last week.

Strategy repurchased $208.2 million in STRC and spent about $65.5 million buying 811 Bitcoin (BTC) at an average price of $80,846, according to a Monday 8-K filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Strategy sold about 1.18 million MSTR shares for net proceeds of $164 million. About $65.5 million funded its Bitcoin acquisition, while the remaining $98.5 million was allocated to the company’s USD Cash balance, according to the filing. The company held $132.7 million in USD Cash and $4.79 billion in its separate US dollar reserve as of Sunday.

The latest purchases followed about $664 million in STRC buybacks between Oct. 1 and Oct. 25, compared with about $72 million in Bitcoin acquisitions over that period.

Strategy’s STRC preferred stock rose 0.1% in pre-market trading on Monday, to $99.22, or about 0.8% below its $100 target price, according to Yahoo Finance. Strategy’s policy is not to issue new STRC shares below $100, limiting that source of funding while the stock trades below its target.

Another Bitcoin treasury company, Japan’s Metaplanet, reported buybacks of its common shares on Monday. It spent about 25.27 billion yen ($160 million) to buy back 96.45 million shares between Oct. 14 and Saturday, representing roughly 7.1% of its issued shares.

#4997. The Ethical Dilemma of Therapists Who Don’t Work With Autistic People

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Recently, I attended a social gathering with a group of mental health providers. As people were talking, I heard someone make the comment, “Oh, I don’t work with autistic people.” I was not surprised by this comment, as I have heard many colleagues say similar things in a number of professional settings over the years. I was also not surprised to observe that most of the other therapists present either offered neutral responses or agreed that they too didn’t work with autistic people.

As an autistic provider and disability rights advocate, I knew I needed to take action. After this incident, I began including an exercise in a training I offer on the intersectionality of neurodevelopmental disabilities and mental health struggles. I have people write down a minority population, then ask them to fill in the following sentence with the group that they chose: “I don’t work with _____ people.”

While most mental health professionals have no objections to someone stating that they don’t work with autistic people, they become quite uncomfortable when they are asked to say, “I don’t work with Black people,” “I don’t work with gay people,” etc., because this statement suddenly feels like an ethics violation.

Someone excluding clients due to their race, ethnicity, gender, or other minority identity would not be tolerated by colleagues; the decision could even lead to serious professional consequences. If this is the case for other minorities, why does the profession look the other way when many providers routinely exclude clients based on their disabilities? One study by Cantor et al. (2020), for example, found that after calling more than 8000 mental health clinics across the US, only 47% would take a referral for a child with autism.

Over the course of history, neurodevelopmentally disabled people have been othered by society. Up until the last few decades, people with neurodevelopmental disabilities (ND) who had high support needs or could not mask fully were often put in institutions, hidden away from the rest of society. Gen X is the first generation whose disabled members have been allowed to live fully in their communities. Because of this, mental healthcare has all but ignored this population. There are few evidence-based mental health treatment modalities for autistic people or people with intellectual disabilities because researchers have only recently begun to study the topic in depth. There is also little instruction in mental health training programs about ND.

It’s no wonder that so many therapists feel unequipped to treat this community.

There is another reason why no one objected when that colleague stated that they don’t work with autistic people. This reason has to do with competency. The NASW Code of Ethics contains the following ethical principle, “Social workers practice within their areas of competence and develop and enhance their professional expertise.” If our mental health training programs are not ensuring that professionals are instructed on how to treat autistic and intellectually disabled clients with co-occurring mental health struggles, then it makes sense that they would feel that they were not competent to do so. If the therapist does not feel competent, they would avoid treating the client in order to avoid an ethical violation.

The problem with using competence to dismiss the responsibility of treating a minority population that tends to struggle with mental health at significantly higher rates than the general population is that it becomes a social justice concern that violates other ethical principles. Again, using The NASW Code of Ethics, this becomes a violation of the following ethical principles:

This ethical dilemma isn’t exclusive to social workers. The American Counseling Association Code of Ethics values professional competence, but also has principles that create a dilemma.

In my intersectionality training, after completing the exercise described above, I ask the following discussion question: “When is it responsible practice to refer a neurodivergent person to a specialist and when is it ableism?”

For those reading this post, I pose the same question.

Competence is important, and research has shown that ND clients do better when therapy is modified to meet their diverse learning needs. However, because the system does so little to train therapists to feel competent, it has created a mental health crisis. For example, autistic people are 9 times more likely to die by suicide than the general population. As a profession, we can no longer sit back and do nothing to meet the needs of ND clients because of a lack of competence. It’s time to learn about the mental health needs of ND people and address the competing principles in this ethical dilemma.

American Counseling Association. (2014). ACA code of ethics. counseling.org/docs/default-source/default-document-library/ethics/2014-aca-code-of-ethics.pdf

Camm-Crosbie, L., Bradley, L., Shaw, R., Baron-Cohen, S., & Cassidy, S. (2019). “People like me don’t get support”: Autistic adults’ experiences of support and treatment for mental health difficulties, self-injury and suicidality. Autism: The International Journal of Research & Practice, 23(6), 1431–1441. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1362361318816053

Cantor, J., McBain, R. K., Kofner, A., Stein, B. D., & Hao Yu. (2020). Fewer than half of US mental health treatment facilities provide services for children with autism spectrum disorder. Health Affairs, 39(6), 968–974. https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2019.01557

Cork, J., (2025). What's your anxiety level? Cognitive behavioral therapy for neurodivergent children and teens with co-occurring anxiety disorders. Routledge Press.

#4995. It Just Got Easier to Get Peptides in the US. Here's What Could Come Next.

Spoiler: More access doesn’t necessarily mean more safety.

ON WEDNESDAY, THE U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced a new policy that makes six experimental peptides more readily available. According to a document released by the HHS, the government will not penalize specialized pharmacies for making and supplying these popular substances to patients with a prescription. The peptides: BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, and TB-500.

This does not mean these particular peptides have been approved for use by the FDA. In fact, none of them have gone through the rigorous human testing required for FDA drug approval. And the new policy is not intended to be permanent. Instead, it allows temporary access as the FDA decides on a longer-term plan for the six peptides. It also includes the caveat that compounders report “serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded,” according to the document.

This topic has been red-hot since July, when the FDA held an advisory committee meeting to consider whether to add these peptides to a list of substances that U.S. compounding pharmacies are allowed to manufacture and supply. These substances are already widely used and obtained on the gray market. If people are going to use them, advocates have argued, it would be safest if those substances came from licensed pharmacies and are used with physician oversight.

Critics, on the other hand—including FDA scientists—are concerned that the government may be opening the floodgates to under-studied and potentially harmful drugs. These substances, they note, have not been fully vetted for safety and effectiveness. And some of these peptides are already being promoted and sold on the basis of scientific claims that experts say are unsupported or questionable.

Here's what could come next, if you're thinking about taking one of these six compounded peptides.

Some parts of the current conversation played out at last month’s PepMed conference in Washington, D.C. A sign pointing guests to the registration table featured a stylized gold peptide overlaid on the white dome of the U.S. Capitol. PepMed’s organizer, the American Academy of Peptide Medicine (AAPM), founded just last year, has already become a major voice in this debate.

In advance of the FDA’s July meeting, AAPM submitted hundreds of pages to a crowded public docket, including information about each of the seven peptides then under review. Several of its advisory board members spoke during the meeting’s public comment sessions. And the group appears to have the ear of the administration. PepMed speakers included the assistant secretary for health, Admiral Brian Christine, and a host of prominent MAHA figures.

The September event opened with an on-the-record media hour, featuring a dozen speakers, including physicians and owners and CEOs of compounding pharmacies and telehealth companies. A recurring theme was the danger of the gray market, where peptide quality can be difficult or impossible to verify and consumers often make treatment decisions without medical oversight—“this is not a victory for patient safety,” said Ricardo Rossello, PhD, a U.S. congressional delegate for Puerto Rico and AAPM advisory board member who co-founded Beijing Prosperous Biopharm, a medical research company.

Many of the speakers also lamented the failure of the U.S. health care system to fully meet the needs of patients, and some of the day’s speakers, including Alex Tatem, MD, an Indiana-based urologist and men’s health specialist with a large YouTube following, presented experimental peptides as part of the solution. “Our established medical system is very much a sick care model,” said Tatem, who serves on the AAPM’s medical advisory board. It’s important to help patients in a health crisis, he told me in an interview. But people want to be proactive about disease prevention. In his view, the peptides under FDA’s consideration can play a role by expanding “the toolkit that’s available to providers.”

At the FDA’s July advisory committee meeting, the agency’s scientists advised against allowing broad access to these peptides, in part because they have not been fully vetted for safety and effectiveness in the kind of long-term, rigorously designed human studies typically required for drug approval.Even at the conference, some doctors acknowledged the evidence gaps. Abud Bakri, MD, works in California as a physician who specializes in caring for hospitalized patients. He also runs a separate medical practice focused on preventive and longevity medicine, and he serves on the Enhanced Games Independent Medical Commission. His interest in peptides has been long-standing enough to predate his medical career.

Bakri, now 33, has been a powerlifter since he was 17. He explained that he has a genetic condition that may increase his risk for ligament injuries. He first used BPC-157 almost a decade ago, and believes the peptide helped him recover faster, though he acknowledges that this is hard to prove definitively, given the absence of well-designed human studies.

If just a fraction of the rat and Petri dish research holds up in humans, BPC-157 could be an incredibly helpful drug in the ICU, he told me at the conference, during an interview at an outdoor dining area. But ideally, he says, its effectiveness should be proven before it’s used in this setting and potential side effects should be better understood. “If I’m going to have an honest conversation with a patient,” he said, “I need to be able to fully elucidate the risk, which I can’t for some of these compounds.”

After the conference, I spoke by Zoom with Thomas Kremen, MD, a physician at UCLA Health who works for several athletic teams, including the Los Angeles Chargers and Lakers. Kremen and his colleagues recently reviewed the evidence behind six popular experimental peptides. He and his co-authors seemed unimpressed. “It’s probably not a strong stance to be recommending these things,” he told me.

Would it be accurate for physicians to tell their patients that a peptide like BPC-157 heals tissue?

“Maybe if they're talking about a rat in some study,” he said. “But I think if you're making a claim, you better be able to cite the literature that supports that.”

Right now, not only is there a dearth of high-quality clinical evidence that peptides work and are safe, unsupported claims are being made about these compounds.

For instance, among the documents that AAPM submitted to the FDA’s public docket was a white paper claiming that two experimental peptides—epitalon and BPC-157—are endogenous, indicating they are naturally produced by the body. Similar descriptions can be found on websites for telehealth companies and online peptide vendors suggesting their products are synthetic versions of naturally derived peptides.

Epitalon is a lab-made peptide based on an extract that researchers in the Soviet Union obtained from cattle brains. Terry Roberts, PhD, a researcher who studies epitalon at Brunel University of London, said it’s unclear whether humans produce this peptide. As far as he’s aware, no studies have explicitly described its presence in humans.

And BPC-157? The peptide was discovered in gastric juice, said Vince Luca, PhD, a researcher at the Moffitt Cancer Center in Florida. Yet 35 years after its discovery, nobody has found a gene that encodes for it—it could have come from a microbe or from food. It’s not impossible that the body produces BPC-157, said Luca, but he thinks it’s unlikely. He also says that health care professionals “should know enough not to tell [people] that it's an endogenous peptide” when it is very unlikely to be one. And regardless, he continued, “there are plenty of endogenous peptides that, injected at high concentrations, would have a really negative effect on the body.” In other words, being endogenous alone doesn’t mean it’s safe.

(The American Academy of Peptide Medicine’s press team did not respond to queries asking how the group determined that BPC-157 and epitalon are endogenous.)

“My prediction is that those who are already using the gray market will continue to do so,” said Ryan Beattie, director of business development at Adaptog Research & Life Sciences, a UK-based company that sells experimental peptides. “So I think in the initial term, people will use compounding pharmacies in the US. What I then predict will happen is people will then get used to it, get more aware of it—and then switch to the gray market because of the cost.”

He may be right. For this story, we spoke with two peptide users who had been living with chronic pain, and after trying physical therapy as well as other treatment approaches, turned to the Wolverine stack, a combination of BPC-157 and TB-500. Both said they felt the peptides helped them—and neither was sure they’d switch to compounded versions, which are more expensive than the gray market and aren’t covered by insurance. One of them, Charles A., asked, “What are the hoops and what are the costs going to be?”

A third person, who asked to be referred to as James—the name he uses in online communities—tried an oral version of BPC-157 four years ago and said he hasn’t been the same since then. Shortly after taking the experimental compound, he felt anxiety followed by sensory and emotional numbness that still hasn’t gone away. He also developed an autoimmune condition. Online, he found others with some similar experiences. When he looked carefully at the published research, he concluded that it didn’t match the online hype. “I felt very foolish afterwards.”

Some scientists are continuing to investigate these peptides. At Moffitt, Luca is currently studying BPC-157 and he’s keeping an open mind.

Over the next few months, he and his colleagues plan to run a variety of very basic experiments in which they add the peptide to human cells and see how those cells respond. The results could provide additional insight into what, precisely, this molecule is doing in the body—and they may help explain why users have reported everything from striking benefits to lasting harm.

Perhaps one day, BPC-157 will prove to be an effective drug, said Luca. But for now, his advice is to wait on using it and other experimental peptides: “I just worry that people are a little too cavalier in how these are handled.”

Sara Talpos is a Michigan-based journalist covering biomedical research and public health. She’s written for publications including STAT, Science, and Undark, where she’s a contributing editor.

#4992. Mercado Bitcoin wallets show post-hack transfers after $46M theft

Brazil’s exchange Mercado Bitcoin paused deposits and withdrawals after a security breach, saying customer funds and data were safe.

Mercado Bitcoin, one of Brazil’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges, confirmed a security incident on Monday that blockchain analysts estimated drained more than $46 million from its wallets. Despite the company’s announcement that it had suspended deposits and withdrawals, addresses associated with the incident continued to receive funds for hours afterward.

Senior security engineer at Certik, Dickson Wu, published an initial post-mortem of the incident, saying the attackers “picked at eight small chains for four hours,” including Base, Optimism and Arbitrum. The attack then moved to the company’s main hot wallets before transferring tiny amounts of Ether (ETH) from 27,160 different addresses.

“So whoever did this can also move money out of MB’s customer deposit addresses,” he wrote.

Security firms have stated the hack was carried out through standard transfers rather than a smart contract exploit. Mercado Bitcoin said the breach would have no financial impact on customers.

According to Wu, hours after Mercado Bitcoin announced a temporary suspension of deposits and withdrawals, funds continued to move out of addresses tied to the breach, followed by thousands of small ETH transfers into a single address.

A spokesperson for Mercado Bitcoin told Cointelegraph that customers had suffered no losses and no data had been leaked, but the company did not respond to requests for comment on the continued transfers. A data breach could also trigger notification requirements to Brazil’s data protection authority.

The hack has not yet been attributed to an organized group and remains under investigation.

Of the stolen funds, by 4:42 pm UTC approximately $6.2 million had been frozen by stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle. About $20 million had been transferred into newly created wallets, while over $20 million remained in associated addresses identified by Mercado Bitcoin, including all 106 BTC.

Mercado Bitcoin had 4.5 million users as of July, when stablecoin issuer Tether announced a $20 million investment to support its expansion in tokenization, payments and credit. Another Tether-backed exchange in Latin America, Chile’s Orionx, announced its closure in September after a forensic audit found that more than $7 million in customer assets had moved to wallets outside its control.

The incident comes days after Binance reported a $6.3 billion hack targeting its hot wallets on Thursday. The exchange suspended deposits and withdrawals and pledged to cover customer losses. Binance began resuming withdrawals on Sunday, saying it had replenished 95% of the stolen assets.

#4991. 12 Best Historic Hotels and Airbnbs That Feel Like Time Traveling (2026)

There are plenty of impressive stays out there, no matter your destination of choice. But booking a historic hotel or Airbnb rental with a storied past—tales of tenants, centuries-old architecture, or whatever else might land a property on a local registrar—is the difference between a simple spot to snooze at night and your next dinner party conversation. From former artists’ homes and firehouses to castles and celebrity-studded hotels, we’ve curated several beguiling places around the world to lay your head at night. As is the case with older buildings, some require a bit of flexibility—say, an outdoor shower or a less-than-fully-equipped kitchen—while others offer a portal to the past (some spots on this list predate the 16th century) rich with amenities and luxury.

The following historical hotels and homes have a story to tell, and guests get a front-row seat.

Perks: Shared beach access, in-unit washer and dryer, sound system, indoor fireplace, fire pit

Architect Frank Lloyd Wright built a lot of incredible spaces for others, but this is the very one he contributed to a Life Magazine article back in 1938 as part of a feature about dream homes. The four-bedroom estate is full of windows (the 63-foot living room has an entire wall of them), and each space is bursting with midcentury furniture and decor. Walking into each room feels like unlocking a new level of a time capsule, from the shag-carpeted primary bedroom to the brick-walled kitchen. While spring, summer, and fall are beautiful times to visit Wisconsin, the fire pit (and hammock) outside is still inviting come winter and snow. From $841 per night.

Perks: Badminton net, steam room, gym, BBQ grill, EV charger

This is the perfect pit stop on a road trip through the Highlands. Hidden in the depths of a former abbey, this one-bedroom space used to be the “writing room” for the monastery. The bed is surrounded by stained glass windows, which look out over the gardens and Loch Ness (yes, of Nessie fame). Guests have access to the neighboring Highland Club, which houses an incredible indoor pool, sauna, tennis court, and so much more. While the kitchen and appliances are newer additions, you will find pieces of furniture from the original space peppered throughout the rental (a wooden bench here, a tapestry there). From $468 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, patio, free parking, pool, outdoor shower

If daydreams of your next trip are filled with al fresco dinners, this two-bedroom home will do you one better by adding bird’s-eye ocean vistas to the scene. Once a windmill that used to grind wheat for flour production, it now houses an outdoor kitchen, a bedroom with a view, and an outdoor shower. The scenes from the top bedroom are really something to write home about—wake up to mountain views and the ocean beyond. The pool is the best spot to take in the sunset before retreating to the open-air dining space for good eats and conversation. From $224 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, Wi-Fi, luggage drop-off, radiant heating, fireplace

This historic Airbnb is known as La Romantica, which should tell you all you need to know. The one-bedroom rental can be found in the oldest section of the property (which dates back earlier than the 1400s), there’s a private entrance, ancient stone walls, antique Italian furniture, and a fireplace that’s perfect for fighting off a chilly night. This is a spot where you do a bit of time traveling, both indoors and out when you decide to explore the surrounding UNESCO heritage town, Teggiano, which is known for its museums (the Diocesan Museum, Herb Museum, and Museum of Folk Traditions, to name a few) and its 13 churches. Guests at this one-bedroom stay are located right in the middle of town and within walking distance of everything you’d need, so slipping out for a quick dinner, coffee at one of the cafes, or a sunset stroll along medieval architecture is always on the itinerary. From $154 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, air conditioning, private parking available, fireplace, historic decor

Built in 1884, this was Washington, DC’s first fully African American fire company and the set of a Netflix show: Check out Stay Here, season one, episode eight. Located in the Shaw neighborhood, a historic district, there are plays to attend (Howard Theatre), drinks to be had (Blagden Alley), and music to take in (Eighth Street Lounge and Bar). The five-bedroom rental even has the original fire pole and you can see previous tenants in the photography that decorates the walls. From $860 per night.

Perks: Shared beach access, sound system, exercise equipment, fire pit

Step right into the world of painter Reginald Marsh when you stay at this two-bedroom getaway with forest views. A pond anchors one side of the property, and the expansive lawns are landscaped with long, post-dinner strolls in mind. As secluded as it feels, it’s a short walk to the center of Woodstock and all of its restaurants, bars, cafes, and shops. And while you’re not near any national parks, the home’s private waterfall (you read that correctly) borders a public preserve that’s open for exploring. The library inside will pull you back indoors, though, as will the wood-burning stove on chilly nights. The outdoor dining space is great for summertime grilling, but the full kitchen indoors is a delight to work in. From $619 per night.

Perks: Central location, trendy bars and restaurant, 24-hour fitness center, balcony access, Aqua di Parma and Byredo toiletries

Centrally located in Madrid’s Plaza de las Cortes, the historic Palace Hotel reopened its doors in 2025 to unveil property-wide updates—including its main lobby, dining accommodations, and 470 rooms—the result of a two-year renovation project with reimagined interiors by designer Lázaro Rosa-Violán. Dating back to 1912, The Palace has seen notable guests like Salvador Dalí and Ernest Hemingway, and is even credited as the first hotel in the country to have private toilets in its quarters.

Today, guests can appreciate pieces of the property’s historic past through a modern lens. Surrounded by bespoke fixtures custom designed by Rosa-Violán, vintage tapestries hang with contemporary Joan Miro prints in La Cúpula Restaurant. Inside the inviting suites, updated bathrooms feature original red marble stone reminiscent of Paloma Elsesser’s luxurious tub. Just a five-minute walk away, art aficionados can spend long hours wandering through the Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum and the Prado museum, or take a stroll through El Retiro Park. “The hotel staff at The Palace are some of the friendliest I’ve encountered,” says commerce editor Audrey Lee. “You’ll definitely want to stop by La Cúpula during your trip for an afternoon drink and some bites from the stylish tapas menu. If it’s the right time of day, the room becomes drenched in sunlight through the dome-shaped stained glass ceiling.” From $1,060 per night.

Perks: Spa, fitness center, concierge, Smart TVs, room service

The history of the Waldorf Astoria runs deep. Originally designed in 1893 as two side-by-side hotels built by feuding family members, the collective property was demolished in 1929 to make room for the Empire State Building’s construction. It was reopened in its current Park Avenue location in 1931, breaking records as the largest and tallest hotel in the world (at the time). Its Art Deco architecture and interiors caught the eyes of royals, celebrities, and politicians around the world. The guest book includes names such as Nikola Tesla, Winston Churchill, Zsa Zsa Gabor, the Obamas, and so many more. After being closed for extensive renovations, the property is planning a grand re-opening for Spring 2025. From $1,221 per night.

Perks: Irene Forte spa, indoor lap pool, three on-site restaurants, whisky tasting experience, afternoon tea, views of Edinburgh landmarks

A historic landmark, the Balmoral is widely recognized for its 190-foot clock tower—famously set three minutes fast, except on New Year’s Eve—that has been part of the Edinburgh skyline since opening in the early 1900s. J.K. Rowling even finished the final Harry Potter book on January 11, 2007, in Suite 552—now commemorated with an owl door knocker and an in-room bust of the Greek god Hermes that Rowling signed. “The Balmoral does rest and relaxation like no other through comforting amenities, charming interiors, and hearty cuisine,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “After a long day of taking in Edinburgh’s historic sights, there was nothing I looked forward to more than the treats from turndown service and a long soak in the glossy marble tub.” Guests also return for the sprawling bedrooms, some of which frame picturesque views of Edinburgh Castle. The stays showcase cozy design with contemporary wallpaper prints, surprisingly neutral plaid furniture, and ultrasoft wool bed covers. From $399 per night.

Perks: Presidential, royal, and celebrity clientele; iconic Bemelmans Bar; walking distance to Central Park

Nestled on 76th Street off Madison Avenue, the Carlyle first opened its doors in 1930. Since then, presidents, royalty, and movie stars have all sought refuge in the hallowed hotel. “You can have breakfast next to Daniel Patrick Moynihan or Tom Ford,” Los Angeles–based designer and AD100 Hall of Famer Michael S. Smith once described. “It's like a big hotel in a small town, the grande dame of New York.” The interiors blend Art Deco touches and New York eclecticism with classic architecture through a layered mix of vintage-inspired furniture silhouettes, contemporary art, and splashy chandeliers. One of the hotel’s top attractions for locals and hotel guests alike is the iconic Bemelmans Bar, outfitted with whimsical wall murals by Madeline author and illustrator Ludwig Bemelmans. The classic martini is a failsafe order, though you could go for the namesake Madeline's Vesper or Bobby’s Manhattan (an homage to cabaret singer Bobby Short, a longtime fixture of Café Carlyle, another classic destination within the Carlyle). From $1,323 per night.

Celebrating its 100th birthday this year, Hotel Figueroa was founded in partnership with The Young Women's Christian Association (YWCA) as a safe haven for solo female travelers. The Downtown Los Angeles fixture was the first property that allowed unaccompanied women to check in without a male chaperone—something most hotels prohibited at the time. Today, Spanish Revival design influences flourish in the space: Expect curated art (exclusively by female artists), sophisticated tilework, and modern furnishings. As you dip in the coffin-shaped pool straight from the 1920s while surrounded by 50-year-old cacti, enjoy craft cocktails and bites from the poolside bar, La Casita. For a more substantial meal, the restaurant-in-residence Florence by the Water serves up Italian classics. From $229 per night.

Perks: Proximity to landmarks, celebrity guest roster, traditional afternoon tea, live music, private tours and experiences available upon request

Widely recognized as London’s oldest luxury hotel, updates like glossy marble bathrooms, vibrant textiles, and mahogany walk-in closets have breathed new life into the historic stay. At the same time, homages to the original architecture—in stained-glass windows, untouched entryways, and wrought-iron façade detailing—forge bonds to its heritage. “You might think the main attraction of Brown’s is its proximity to landmarks like Buckingham Palace and Hyde Park, but it’s actually the inviting staff and dapper design that make this stay more like a home than a stopover,” says Lee. Past literary guests of note include Rudyard Kipling, Bram Stoker, Agatha Christie, and Stephen King; King even outlined his bestseller Misery during one of his stays. Situated in the upscale Mayfair neighborhood, world-class shopping and top London museums ensure your agenda stays full. From $966 per night.

Craving an escape? From colorful carry-ons to cleverly designed packing cubes (how did we ever travel without them?), shop everything you need to make the journey in style—and as streamlined and stress-free as possible.

#4987. Pregnant, but Think You Might Already Have Postpartum?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

With heightened attention on postpartum depression, anxiety, and psychosis, a critical truth has been missed: A significant percentage of “postpartum” mental health disorders actually begin in pregnancy.

Often termed PMADs, Perinatal Mood and Anxiety Disorders encompass depressive, anxiety, and bipolar disorders. (The latter is often linked to postpartum psychosis—a rare and poorly treated variant.) The perinatal or peripartum period means “surrounding birth,” and includes the entire pregnancy and year after.

Research suggests that a third of perinatal depression cases begin during pregnancy. Anxiety disorder symptoms during early pregnancy are actually more prevalent than postpartum, with a quarter of pregnant women experiencing anxiety in early pregnancy, dropping to 20 percent during the remaining peripartum. Perinatal obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is experienced by about 8 percent of women during pregnancy, and about twice that number experience it postpartum. New-onset bipolar is rare in the peripartum period, but over 50 percent of women who have bipolar before pregnancy experience at least one episode peri-partally.

Women and their loved ones need to be aware of the risk of early-onset PMADs. Frequently, women have been struggling with anxiety, depression, OCD, or bipolar symptoms for weeks or months before birth, but no one has inquired and women may feel anxious or embarrassed to mention them.

Often, mild PMADs can be treated with individual or group psychotherapy and lifestyle changes like sleep improvement, stress reduction, and social support. But a large proportion of women experiencing PMADs have moderate-to-severe symptoms requiring medication, which many fear or avoid, but shouldn’t because medication saves lives. In the United States alone, the largest causes of maternal death—20 percent—are suicide or overdose linked to PMADs.

Here’s what can help you or a woman you love get the treatment needed:

If you’re pregnant or even considering pregnancy and are also experiencing anxiety, depression, or bipolar symptoms, talk to your provider and find the help you need.

Learn more about psychiatric disorders during pregnancy, and medications during pregnancy, so you’re primed with knowledge. You can even help women following in your footsteps by signing up for the national pregnancy medication registry and contributing to improved medication knowledge for all women, long into the future.

Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health. (2026, July). Maternal Mental Health Fact Sheet. policycentermmh.org/maternal-mental-health-fact-sheet/

#4986. 7 Best Glassware Sets to Elevate Your Tablescape (2026)

You don’t need a perfectly mixed cocktail or an expensive bottle of wine to justify drinking out of the good glasses. Sometimes, a cold glass of water is occasion enough. And if you’re going to reach for the same one several times a day, it might as well be one you enjoy looking at. Picture it now: curved and patterned drinking glasses that can make an everyday meal feel a bit more festive.

Choosing the right glassware is a surprisingly personal affair, though. Some people swear by a barely-there rim; others prefer the reassuring heft of a substantial tumbler. Then there’s the way a glass sits in your hand. These details might seem inconsequential until you find a glass you love drinking from—and suddenly every other one in your arsenal becomes a little less appealing. To make your sips more style-forward, we’ve rounded up a variety of designer water glasses, special-occasion stems, and other favorites you'll want to clear a little cabinet space for.

The generously sized bowls of these LSA International wine glasses leave plenty of room for a proper pour (and an enthusiastic swirl without worrying about spilling over the rim). They’re also made from dishwasher-safe crystalline glass, so you can skip the handwashing once the party wraps up.

If you want to introduce color to your glassware collection but can’t settle on just one shade, this set makes it easy to have a little bit of everything. Estelle Colored Glass’s six Champagne coupes come in an assortment of vibrant hues, so no one has to lose track of their drink at your next dinner party.

Perfectly imperfect is part of the vintage charm of these handblown glasses from il Buco Vita. #4985. Even As a Wicker Man, Alexander Skarsgård’s Got Game. This Scent Will Give You Some Too.

The actor is the face of Valentino’s newest fragrance, Vendetta.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF ANYONE CAN MAKE RATTAN hot, it’s Alexander Skarsgård. The actor’s latest film project, about a craftsman who creates a wicker husband (Skarsgård) for a lonely woman (played by Olivia Colman), has been an unlikely hit since its release in theaters last week. But basket weave isn’t the only material Skarsgård’s rocking—he’s been killing it on the red carpet lately, too.

There was the gold Saint Laurent suit earlier this month at the BFI London Film Festival, the sick Chopova Lowena skirt to promote Wicker at the Los Angeles premiere last week, and the head-to-toe Valentino outfit he wore at the house’s show during Paris Fashion Week. It seems there’s nothing Alexander Skarsgård can’t infuse with his unique brand of Swedish swag.

Shop the new Valentino Vendetta fragrance.

So, it should come as no surprise when Valentino tapped the 50-year-old star as one of the faces of its brand-new fragrance pillar, Vendetta (alongside Dakota Johnson for the women’s version). Unlike Valentino’s most famous scent family, Born in Roma, which features a spiked pyramid design, Vendetta’s bottle pays homage to the brand’s classic V motif, with a rich, sensual juice created by master perfumer Marie Salamagne.

You’ll get the sensuality from the campaign imagery, photographed by iconic duo Inez & Vinoodh, and the epic accompanying video, directed by French filmmaker Romain Gavras, but what about the fragrance itself?

“It has a boldness and a kind of self-assertive quality to it,” Skarsgård tells me when I ask him to describe the scent. “It’s not quite as heavy as I thought it would be. That first note of ginger has a lightness to it and then it evolves into those richer, deeper notes that last longer.”

For his part, Skarsgård says he’s a signature scent kind of guy—a far cry from the scentmaxxing approach of today’s TikTokers, who douse themselves in enough cologne to create their own noxious atmosphere.

“I’m a proponent of finding your fragrance and sticking with it,” he says. “You become associated with that smell, it becomes part of who you are.”

That’s not to say he hasn’t had his share of missteps. Born in Stockholm, Skarsgård began acting at a young age—his first film role came when he was just seven—but quit as a teenager to join the Swedish navy and, eventually, attend university. Along the way, he learned some valuable fragrance lessons, as most guys do. “I think when I was a teenager, I overdid it a lot,” he says. “You want to marry your scents, so it’s a combination of the fragrance and your own natural scent.”

A woody-spicy addition to the Valentino fragrance family, Vendetta is the first new scent pillar from the brand since its blockbuster Born in Roma.

It’s quite an evolution for a lad who equates childhood with the unmistakable aroma of sausage. When I ask Skarsgård about his first connection to fragrance—that unmistakably transformative power of scent—it’s the sausage factory that faced his front door.

“To this day, it really brings me back, and they’re fond memories,” he says. “Whenever I smell sausage, I’m an eight-year-old again. I’m getting ready for school, seeing my buddies, thinking about this girl I had a crush on. It strikes a chord.”

Of course, processed meat isn’t a key part of the olfactive experience of Vendetta Uomo. It opens with a sharp note of sparkling ginger with the typical brightness of a top note. From there, a warm, rich cinnamon liquor accord envelops the nose and gives way to earthy, grounding patchouli and woods. It’s at turns inviting and accessible while still drawing you in with something seductive and unique.

It’s sex in a spritz, the idea being that you too can have the appeal of a 6'4" Norse god. Ironically, Skarsgård’s everyday life couldn’t be more different from what he says most people see when he’s walking the red carpet or strutting his stuff on screen.

“When I’m not working, I’m trying to spend as little time as possible thinking about [my skincare and sartorial choices],” he says. “It’s all about comfort. I’ve been on a shoot for four months and I’ve been wearing the same shorts and flip-flops for months.”

But isn’t that part of the appeal of a fragrance—the ability to be a different person, someone out of your ordinary? Sure, you could be wearing a pair of sweats and a hat, but with a spray of Vendetta, you’re suddenly wearing a leopard-print overcoat on top of it.

It’s a good look. Just ask Alexander Skarsgård.

#4983. Coinbase hit with 50% price target cut as post-earnings rout deepens

Slowing trading activity and fallout from the Binance hack are clouding Coinbase’s revenue prospects, prompting Morgan Stanley to lower its rating on the stock.

Investment bank Morgan Stanley turned bearish on Coinbase (COIN) on Monday, cutting its price target by more than half as it warned that the cryptocurrency exchange’s profits could recover more slowly than expected.

Analyst Michael Cyprys lowered the stock’s price target from $258 to $120, a cut of about 53%, citing recent trading trends, a softer revenue outlook and uncertainty in the crypto market following Binance’s $6.3 billion hack, according to a Monday report.

The bank still sees Coinbase as one of the strongest competitors in crypto but expects profits to recover more slowly than previously forecast, putting further pressure on its share price.

The downgrade comes days after Coinbase reported a roughly 34% year-over-year decline in third-quarter net revenue to $1.16 billion on Oct. 29. The exchange posted $719 million in net income, largely driven by gains on cryptocurrency investments, while adjusted net income was $78 million.

The company’s earnings sparked a selloff in crypto-linked stocks on Friday, with its shares falling more than 13% in midday trading amid the fallout from the Binance hack. Circle shares declined more than 9%, while Strategy fell about 8%.

Coinbase shares extended their losses on Monday, dropping more than 3.3% to $138 at the time of writing, according to Yahoo Finance data.
