#4982. This Serene 540-Square-Foot Apartment With Sweeping NYC Views Is Designed Down to an Eighth of an Inch

AD’s Small Spaces series is a celebration of small homes—1,000-square-feet or fewer!—with big design ideas. From Manhattan apartments to Milanese micro-homes, each one is proof that you don’t need a sprawling space to show off your personal style.

When a Los Angeles–based startup consultant decided to establish a more permanent foothold in New York, he searched for a place that felt different from his bright Southern California home. For him, being bicoastal meant embracing the best of each, and so, when in the Big Apple, he wanted the apartment to feel unmistakably like New York. That, he said, meant something “moodier, masculine, and more dramatic.” He landed on a Chelsea studio with sweeping views of the Empire State Building and Hudson Yards.

The 540-square-foot apartment, however, didn’t yet fit the bill. An oddly configured layout, coupled with a series of ad hoc renovations (including the discovery of a wall stuffed with Styrofoam), had left the space cramped and dated. That’s when Dyali, the studio founded by 2026 New American Voice Rahul Ghera, stepped in. Working within such a tight footprint, Ghera knew that every design element had to be exacting. The goal, he says, was “amplifying functionality day through evening”—from strategically placed storage to areas for entertaining friends and working comfortably from home.

In the living room of the Chelsea studio designed by Dyali, a rift oak coffee table from 1stDibs grounds the space, flanked by a 1960s armchair by Jindrich Halabala and a foldable chair by Carl Hansen & Son. A custom sofa upholstered in Larsen’s Asante in linen runs along the wall, and a sand-colored rug by Nordic Knots unites the dining and living areas. The project construction is by Homlistic.

In the kitchen, walnut cabinetry is set off by a Calacatta Viola marble countertop from SMC Stone and a Dornbracht Elio fitting in stainless steel. Open shelving makes the room feel more spacious and everyday dishes are within reach.

“It’s almost like a hospitality project in a way—a personalized suite that’s your own place,” says Ghera. “Just with Jay-Z singing ‘I’m in New York’ views.”

A hotel-like emphasis on function guided the design. What began as a solution for storage unlocked one of the apartment’s defining features: a wall-to-wall cabinet running from the bedroom through the living room that doubles as a dresser and a place for games, books, and other odds and ends. To carry the cabinet through, Ghera widened an existing opening between the two rooms. Keeping the cabinet horizontal and continuous made the space feel “wider and bigger,” Ghera says, and drew the eye to the views and light from the windows. The horizon line where the cabinet meets the windowsill, he adds, is like a “border around the home” that almost “hugs you.”

The entry’s deep walnut closets and storage, Ghera says, “serve a pantry-like function,” holding items such as shoes, suitcases, linens, and cleaning supplies. “What I wanted to do is have that walnut turn the corner and just continue into the kitchen.” Courtney Heron’s painting of a domestic scene, Company at the Table, adds warmth to the space.

Ghera says he “intentionally wanted to create a dining feel,” while preserving the room’s openness. The lean form of the USM table allows you to “still see through it.” Audo’s Ready dining chairs in stained oak, upholstered in Audo bouclé, surround it. Beyond the table, a USM Haller cabinet in brown metal offers a casual perch for objets and sculpture, such as a Brutalist bronze sculpture from Mantiques Modern. Glassware, including a vintage Christian Dior ice bucket and lowball and highball glasses, rounds out the display.

The project, Ghera explains, was “an incredible puzzle to solve with a kind of quirky floor plan to start.” His answer was a restrained yet expressive material palette, anchored by rich walnut millwork and reflective surfaces that tie the rooms together. In the galley kitchen, a stainless-steel backsplash plays against the grain of the walnut cabinetry and lets the room feel more expansive than it is.

The millwork takes center stage in the bedroom, where a large custom mirror, bed, headboard, and nightstands, all in walnut, read as one cohesive piece. To make the most out of the existing square footage, Ghera opted for a platform bed and floating nightstands to avoid clutter and improve flow. A vintage Turkish kilim lumbar pillow in deep crimson, and bedding in shirt blue and red, add whimsy to the otherwise quiet room.

A walnut-framed mirror in the bedroom has an outsize effect. It “nearly doubled the square footage of what the apartment feels like,” says Ghera. “It continues the bouncing of light…and it just feels a little bit airier.”

The entry meets the client’s practical needs. A roomy storage cabinet in smoked oak from Ferm Living serves as a catchall for keys and everyday items, and a lacquered wood mirror from West Elm leans against the wall beside a burgundy linen ottoman from de Le Cuona.

Floating night tables and a custom cabinet along the window provide ample storage. Bedside, Stemlite table lamps in pebble gray by Gubi softly illuminate the space. Sara Marlowe Hall’s pastel drawings, Red 1 & Red 2, play off the crimson vintage Turkish kilim lumbar pillow

In the living room, comfort and flexibility were musts. The client, who likes to host friends for drinks or dinner, needed a space that could easily adapt to gatherings of varying sizes. A custom, deep-seated sofa upholstered in Larsen’s Asante in Linen fabric fits several guests and offers a cozy spot for overnight visitors. Versatile furnishings like the Cuba Lounge Chair by Carl Hansen & Son can be folded up and tucked away in the closet to make room for larger parties.

Fitting a dining area into a studio of this size was a true exercise in spatial gymnastics. “It still kind of blows my mind,” says Ghera, “but it works.” A sleek USM dining table topped with oak veneer forms its own “contained” island where a suspension lamp hangs deliberately low to serve as a “focal point,” Ghera says.

Rather than fret over the windowless bathroom, Ghera chose to “lean into it.” “Small rooms look incredible when they’re a little darker,” he says. Outer Clé’s Lido Aperto Bouchon tiles in matte rare garnet wrap the space, and a custom sink pairs Calacatta Viola marble with a stainless-steel base, made from “every square inch” of the stone used in the kitchen.

As a friend told the client, the “pièce de résistance” of the apartment is the bathroom, and he couldn’t agree more. Oxblood garnet tiles envelop the space, from floor to ceiling. Lighting spills from above and below the medicine cabinet and washes down from a cove in the shower. “It really just feels like you are cradled in this space,” says Ghera. “It’s a little sexy.” Reeded glass adds a hint of transparency. “It’s like showering in the world’s coolest hotel,” says the client.

Working within the constraints of such a small studio left little margin for error. Rather than letting it faze him, Ghera worked “down to the eighth of an inch,” he says. “You really have to be so honed in on the tiny details…and intentional about the things you do.”

#4980. Crypto investigators flag suspected $106M theft, $786K Solana bot drain

A European entity may have lost $106 million from exchange accounts, while a wallet associated with a Solana arbitrage bot may have lost another $786,000.

An unidentified entity in the European Union may have lost more than $106 million from accounts at multiple cryptocurrency exchanges on Sunday, according to blockchain investigator ZachXBT.

In a Monday post, ZachXBT said funds suspected to have been stolen were withdrawn in USDC and USDT before being moved through several cryptocurrencies and blockchains.

The suspected attacker swapped USDC for Ether (ETH), used instant exchange services including WellWallet and Kyrrex, and converted funds into Monero (XMR) through the swap service Wagyu.

The suspected attacker remains unidentified, though ZachXBT said the movement of funds pointed away from a link to North Korea’s Lazarus Group. The affected entity and exchanges involved have not been publicly named.

ZachXBT identified 11 wallet addresses associated with the funds.

The reported theft follows the $6.3 billion Binance hack on Oct. 29, which the FBI has attributed to North Korean hackers known as “TraderTraitor,” a group linked to Lazarus. The attack was the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

Related: Binance net outflows surge to $5.8B as withdrawals resume after record hack

A wallet associated with King, an automated trading bot on Solana, may have lost about $786,000 on Monday, according to pseudonymous blockchain monitoring account Onchain Lens.

King is an arbitrage bot, a software that automatically buys cryptocurrency in one market and sells it in another to profit from price differences. Onchain Lens told Cointelegraph the funds moved through several Solana wallets before being transferred to Ethereum using Mayan, a service for moving assets between blockchains. It said the rapid transfers suggested an attempt to conceal the funds’ origin and a possible wallet compromise.

King’s operator has not confirmed a compromise.

“Our report is based on unusual fund movements, rapid transfers and the subsequent cross-chain movement of funds, which we believe indicates an attempt to obscure their origin,” Onchain Lens told Cointelegraph. “This pattern strongly suggests a potential wallet compromise.”

#4979. Do Your Muscles Need a ‘Creatine Washout?’ It Depends.

The benefits might be more mental than physical.

CREATINE IS THE prom king of social media—everyone’s talking about it. And not always nice things, either. Because for all the (very warranted) complements about how creatine can help you grow stronger, there’s also some (baseless) behind-the-back whispers about how it can make your hair fall out, poison you with heavy metals, and yes even kill you.

Between this polarization, there’s the seemingly reasonable personal stance of Andrew Huberman, PhD: Take creatine, but also take a creatine break.

Just in case you’re unfamiliar, a Huberman is a neuroscientist and associate professor in the Departments of Neurobiology and Ophthalmology at Stanford University School of Medicine. And he only hosts one of the most popular health podcasts of all time, Huberman Lab. When Huberman says anything about anything, people listen.

So when Huberman posted that he does a “creatine washout” every four months “just to see what effect it continues to have over time,” you have to wonder.

IT’S THE TIME period after you stop supplementing with creatine. The term is used frequently in scientific research that assesses the effects of creatine supplementation, often in athletic performance studies.

But, admittedly, there aren’t that many studies that look at the creatine washout phase itself. The most recent goes all the way back to 2004: “Effects of repeated creatine supplementation on muscle, plasma, and urine creative levels.”

In that study researchers found that levels of muscle phosphocreatine—that’s the amount of creatine stored within muscle cells—did not return to pre-supplementation baselines even after a 30-day washout period.

Since that 2004 study, there hasn’t been any supportive—or contradictory—science, but the lead author says the findings hold up more than 20 years later.

“Four to six weeks is a typical response and depends on dietary creatine, response to supplement, etc.,” says Eric Rawson, PhD, FACSM, Chair of the Department of Health, Nutrition, and Exercise Science at Messiah University, and a co-author of the 2004 washout study.

MAYBE, BUT NOT for reasons you might think.

“Questions about creatine washout and/or cycling supplementation are best handled from both physiological and behavioral perspectives,” says Rawson. “When I am asked about washout and cycling, I always ask people if they have similar concerns about their multivitamin. Or their calcium supplements. Or whey protein.”

Meaning, do you have the same washout concerns about creatine as you do your other supplements? Probably not.

“There appears to be a lingering concern about long-term creatine supplementation that is not supported by data.”

That said, Rawson says that some people, including many athletes, can feel overwhelmed by demands of maintaining their fitness edge—to the point where it’s good to take a break for mental health.

“Taking an off-season break from some of the usual routines, which includes, training, meal frequency, macro-nutrient intake goals, and the daily dietary supplement routine, can provide a break and perhaps some relief from the usual routine,” he says.

How long a break is sort of up to you and your long-term goals. But let your body and brain be the judge of that—not whatever you hear on social.

#4978. Why High Self-Esteem Doesn't Guarantee Self-Acceptance

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Can you feel good about yourself and still struggle to accept yourself? Yes. Self-esteem and self-acceptance are related, but they aren’t the same. Understanding the difference may help explain why someone who seems confident can still feel utterly shaken by a setback—and why unconditional self-acceptance can be a steadier foundation.

Western societies pay lots of attention to self-esteem. People seek therapy to raise it, parents worry about harming their children’s self-esteem, and partners may blame relationship problems on low self-esteem. A healthy self-esteem can benefit mental health. One meta-analysis of 77 studies on depression and 18 on anxiety found that higher self-esteem predicted less subsequent depression and anxiety.

But self-esteem has a less familiar cousin: Self-acceptance. If self-esteem is a positive evaluation of your worth, self-acceptance means accepting yourself as a whole person, including your strengths, weaknesses, and feelings. The late psychologist Albert Ellis coined the term unconditional self-acceptance, or USA, to mean accepting yourself without making your worth depend on success, failure, imperfections, or other people’s approval.

Research suggests that self-esteem and USA overlap but are not identical. In one study, USA was associated with less anxiety, better moods after setbacks, and lower narcissism, even after accounting for self-esteem, suggesting that self-esteem and USA might reflect different pathways to psychological health.

If the two attributes are related but distinct, what might different combinations look like? Imagine a matrix with self-esteem on one axis and unconditional self-acceptance on the other.

The grounded self has high self-esteem and high self-acceptance. The imperfectionist has low self-esteem but high USA: They may have a poor evaluation of themselves, yet accept themselves as a person. The self-critic has low levels of both. But it's the conditional achiever, who has high self-esteem but low USA, that fascinates me most.

Wait—how can someone feel good about themselves but struggle to accept themselves? Two patterns may help explain this.

Pursuing healthy self-esteem is worthwhile. But I’d argue that embracing unconditional self-acceptance matters even more.

First, raising your self-esteem can be difficult. If you believe a lot has gone wrong in your life, you may feel like you have compelling evidence for a negative view of yourself. That view can change, but it could take time. Learning to accept your imperfections, failures, and weaknesses may be a more manageable starting point than trying to feel good about yourself.

Second, life is uncertain. Career success, physical appearance, and relationships can change. People lose jobs, retire, age, and sometimes lose a partner. Accepting yourself without conditions gives you a steadier point of reference through those changes—a north star that helps you find your way when life shifts.

Third, paradoxically, unconditional self-acceptance could make self-improvement less threatening. If failure feels like proof that you’re worthless, it makes sense to avoid trying. But when a setback doesn’t determine your worth, you can pursue a goal without living under constant threat. Accepting a weakness doesn’t mean refusing to change it; it can actually make change feel safer.

Here are seven ways to begin practicing unconditional self-acceptance.

Develop a mantra that captures unconditional self-acceptance. Below is one I’ve developed. If it speaks to you, feel free to use or adapt it. Say it to yourself every morning. Let the words soak into your mind before beginning each day:

I am human. I am imperfect. I am whole. I accept my past. I accept my flaws. I accept myself.

Practicing unconditional self-acceptance can be liberating. It replaces the endless task of proving you’re impressive enough with something steadier: improving what you can, accepting what you can’t change, and not using either as a yardstick to measure whether you’re worthy. That’s a vision of a life worth embracing.

This post follows up on my earlier post on why loving yourself first is a relationship myth. If you appreciated this piece, you might also enjoy my newsletter on the science and practice of gratitude.

Chamberlain, J. M., & Haaga, D. A. F. (2001). Unconditional self-acceptance and psychological health. Journal of Rational-Emotive & Cognitive-Behavior Therapy, 19(3), 163–176. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1011189416600

Crocker, J., & Knight, K. M. (2005). Contingencies of Self-Worth. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 14(4), 200-203. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0963-7214.2005.00364.x

#4977. AI poses greater threat to Bitcoin than quantum computing, Swan founder says

The Swan Bitcoin founder warned that hackers are using large language models to exploit security flaws with just a few prompts.

Artificial intelligence poses a more immediate threat to Bitcoin security than quantum computing, according to Swan Bitcoin founder Cory Klippsten, who warned that hackers are increasingly using AI to exploit vulnerabilities as crypto exchanges face a string of security breaches.

Speaking on Cointelegraph’s Chain Reaction, Klippsten dismissed much of the concern surrounding quantum computing as speculative, arguing that advances in large language models present a more pressing challenge as attackers use the technology to probe security weaknesses.

The warning comes as Brazil’s Mercado Bitcoin suspended deposits and withdrawals on Monday following a security incident, with researchers estimating that more than $46 million had left its wallets. Just days earlier, exchange Binance lost $6.3 billion in an Oct. 29 hack that the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) attributed to North Korean hackers.

Klippsten estimated that quantum computers capable of threatening Bitcoin’s cryptography remain at least a decade away, potentially longer. He argued that the network could adopt quantum-resistant protections if the threat became credible, but said rushing to implement them now would introduce unnecessary complexity.

He warned that cryptocurrency companies cannot rely on hastily developed software when safeguarding customer assets. “You need to actually know what the hell you’re doing from a security standpoint,” he said.

Klippsten also suggested that some cryptocurrency startups and investors had used fears surrounding quantum computing to attract funding, characterizing much of the discussion as fear, uncertainty and doubt (“FUD”) rather than an imminent security concern.

From Joonbyrd to L’Occitane, here’s what formulas actually work.

I’ll be the first to admit it: I spend a copious amount of money on spa treatments and refining my at-home skincare routine. From my $78 Isdin sunscreen and Paula’s Choice Exfoliant to biweekly facials, my focus has always been on achieving clear, wrinkle-free skin without injections. But after chatting with double board-certified dermatologist Serena Mraz, MD, I realized that I’ve been neglecting my hands for far too long.

As a New Yorker, I take the subway several times a day for work, events, and to meet up with friends. I’m also a germaphobe and rely on hand sanitizer or harsh soap in office and restaurant bathrooms after riding the train. As a result, my hands are inevitably dry, dull, and rough. That's not exactly the look I’m going for as our beauty editor. It also doesn’t help that Dr. Mraz says cumulative sun damage, including dark spots and wrinkles, is one of the biggest culprits in showing my age. Wait, what do you mean my age didn’t pause during the pandemic? “Your skin records sun exposure like your car tallies mileage,” dermatologist Hadley King, MD, previously told me about how skincare changes in your 40s. “You can't turn back the odometer on your car, and you can't turn back sun damage from your skin."

Hand creams provide instant hydration and support the skin barrier, helping me achieve the baby-soft skin of my dreams. I’ve noticed that investing in my favorites lets me reapply less frequently and use a smaller amount of product, ultimately trimming my cost per use. It’s beauty math, ladies!

Creams, such as L'Occitane and Beau Domaine, are the thickest and most nourishing type of hand care products. Dr. Mraz is a fan of creams because they’re packed with more lipids than water, which helps deliver the best moisture. The downside is that they take longer to rub into your hands and across larger areas like your arms.

Ointments, such as Aquaphor and Vaseline, are versatile, fragrance-free moisturizers that relieve dryness without causing irritation, says dermatologist and clinical professor of dermatology Gary Goldenberg, MD. They’re made with petrolatum to keep your skin moist, which helps prevent wounds from drying out and forming a scab. These are especially useful when you have super cracked skin.

Lotions are thinner and more fluid than creams. Some are even runny, but don’t worry: the right lotions still restore moisture for instant relief and prevent dryness. Notably, our best overall pick—Joonbyrd Wonder·Land Hand Lotion—has a luxurious consistency that feels and smells like it belongs in a spa. It’s so enjoyable, I use it all over my body and notice instant hydration without leaving residue on my clothes.

The dermatologists I consulted recommend moisturizing ingredients glycerin, shea butter, and cocoa butter—they can be found in many of our suggestions, like Aquaphor and Juara.

Hyaluronic acid is another standout that acts as a moisture magnet, holding up to 1,000 times its weight in water. It’s so epic that dermatologists recently told me you can even use hyaluronic acid on your hair and scalp.

As our fragrance-obsessed beauty editor, I also factored in the scent profiles. While all of these hand creams smell good, I also highlighted the key notes that make each one stand out. Homecourt's five impressive aromas—ranging from roses to citrus and aromatic—and Juara's Bali-inspired coconut blend are some of my favorites. If scents aren’t your thing, opt for Nécessaire. What it lacks in aroma, it makes up for in skin-nourishing and soothing ingredients, including ceramides and niacinamide.

To kick off this evaluation process, I went directly to medical experts about their no-fail hand creams.

Ready to make dry hands a thing of the past? Look no further than these eight expert-approved hand creams worthy of a spot in your routine.

Joonbyrd offers two hand care products: the featured Wonder·Land Hand Lotion and the Confetti Sky Hand Treatment. TBH, the latter is compact and more travel-friendly, but I genuinely love the Hand Lotion so much that I apply it to my body. My picky, scent-averse mom also found the sophisticated warm and sweet gourmand notes appealing.

Aroma aside, the formulation and ingredient list are on point. The fast-absorbing, nourishing lotion is made with all my favorite heavy hitters: ceramides, amino acids, and niacinamide. They’re basically a trifecta of skincare goodness that repair my skin barrier and hydrate.

Joonbyrd says this hand lotion moisturizes for up to 48 hours. However, I’m a frequent handwasher, so I can’t speak to going two full days without soap and water on my skin. Personally, I noticed my hands felt softer after a week of consistent reapplication, and I can use this lotion twice daily afterward.

I initially tested it for one month straight before comparing it to other picks. (More on that shortly!) Since then, I’ve been reaching for it almost daily for a year. It offers long-lasting hydration and skin barrier support. Joonbyrd is so effective at leaving my skin softer and more supple that even acquaintances have noticed how soft my hands feel.

To ensure others received a fair assessment during the second month of my testing process, I evaluated how Joonbyrd compared with other options.

Joonbyrd wins over the French staple, as it’s lighter and features a modern formula that strengthens the skin barrier. L’Occitane remains a beauty classic, but if you want something new that you can apply all over your body, opt for Joonbyrd.

Go with the latter if you’re a price-conscious shopper or just super sensitive to scents. Hey, it happens to me during the spring and summer, so I totally get it! Joonbyrd is luxurious—the pretty packaging elevates my vanity setup, and the green, textured exterior helps prevent it from rolling off my table.

Joonbyrd is a non-sticky lotion that absorbs quickly, leaving no pesky residue on my belongings. It’s your best bet when your hands require barrier support and nourishment. Here’s where things get tougher. HomeCourt offers an aspirational, Insta-famous brand vibe, but with hydrating ingredients that enhance my skin. Arguably the most famous hand cream of the bunch, L'Occitane's non-greasy formula has earned plenty of love from our beauty team. So what makes it so iconic? L’Occitane is made with gentle, effective ingredients, such as 20 percent organic shea butter, glycerin, and skin-plumping omegas. Aquaphor and Vaseline are similar drugstore staples—they both use petroleum to lock in moisture and repair the skin barrier. Though Juara doesn't make any specific eczema safety certifications, Dr. Ruth doesn’t mind it for her patients with that skin condition. TBH, my eczema flares up during the winter and seasonal transitions, but this nourishing cream hasn’t caused any sensitivity issues.

#4975. New Jersey drops Coinbase staking order ahead of crypto’s midterm test

New Jersey lifted its staking ban and dropped a $5 million penalty, clearing the way for Coinbase to restore staking access for users in the US state.

New Jersey’s securities regulator has rescinded its 2023 cease-and-desist order against Coinbase’s staking service, lifting a ban that stopped residents staking new funds on the exchange for over three years.

The Oct. 30 notice, signed by Acting Bureau Chief Keith A. Alt, withdrew the order and its $5 million penalty without prejudice and without a ruling on the merits. The wording leaves the Bureau of Securities free to bring a fresh enforcement action against Coinbase in the future.

Coinbase disclosed the move in its third-quarter filing, stating the regulator informed the company on Oct. 29 of its plan to rescind. CEO Brian Armstrong said New Jersey users would regain staking access “very soon”.

California, Maryland, Wisconsin and Washington are still pursuing enforcement actions against the exchange with cases against the its staking services.

Staking involves committing cryptocurrency to help validate transactions and secure a blockchain in exchange for rewards. Companies like Coinbase handle the process for customers and take a share of the rewards as a fee.

California led the ten-state task force behind the 2023 actions, which covered more than 600,000 accounts held by Californians.

Like New Jersey, California and Wisconsin and Maryland banned Coinbase from new staking while their cases ran. Washington’s regulator allows staking but the ongoing case seeks to impose a $4 million fine on the exchange.

Coinbase estimates that California users have missed out on over $89 million in staking rewards since 2023, against more than $15 million in New Jersey.

The decision came ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, with prediction markets favoring Democrats to win the Senate control. A Democratic majority would put Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a prominent crypto critic, in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee, while Sen. Cynthia Lummis, a leading Republican advocate for the industry, is set to retire in January 2027.

New Jersey’s reversal came under Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill, who voted for both the CLARITY and GENIUS bills as a House member. The state’s Democratic senator, Cory Booker, also helped negotiate market structure legislation, though he opposed advancing CLARITY in September.

The industry has sought to build support across party lines ahead of the midterms. Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs are backing 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats in House races, while New Jersey’s Josh Gottheimer has also received crypto-industry support. The number of members of Congress with an A rating from advocacy group Stand With Crypto has risen to 332, up from 96 when the group launched in 2023, according to Reuters.

#4974. I’m a Doctor and I Won’t Touch Honey Packs. Here’s What I Do Before Sex Instead

Ahead, three tried-and-true strategies for better, longer-lasting erections.

IF YOU HAVE difficulty getting erections or simply want to spruce up your sex life, chances are you’ve heard about honey packs. The sachets of the sweet stuff are all over social media, promising enhanced sexual performance through stronger, long-lasting erections.

At first glance, you might find this a “natural” alternative for young guys who don’t want pills or painful-sounding ED procedures like shock wave therapy. After all, the packets do feature pictures of honey and bees swarming on honeycombs, and honey is usually one of the first ingredients—a food many dudes already drizzle in oatmeal and tea. What could go wrong?

MH did a deep dive last year into whether honey packs actually work. The TL;DR version is that despite the alluring promise of near-instant, rock-hard erections, you’re really taking a gamble on what you’re putting in your body. Natural ingredients like honey and ginseng provide a “trivial” performance-enhancing effect and multiple honey pack supplement companies have been flagged by the FDA for having hidden and unknown dosages of ingredients not included in the label, like tadalafil (the active ingredient in Cialis), sildenafil (the active ingredient in Viagra), and acetaminophen.

That’s why doctors have big safety concerns about honey packs, says Scott Miller, MD, a urologist and director of robotic surgery at Wellstar Health System. “If they can’t tell me what’s in them, then it’s an absolute no.” So if honey packs are out, what are some ways to help you get hard and stay hard? We turned to the experts, asking urologists what they do to prepare in lieu of popping a pack.

HONEY PACKS (AND even gas station dick pills) aren’t worth your time or money. But not all supplements need to be ruled out, says Philip Werthman, MD, a urologist and director of the Center for Male Reproductive Medicine and Vasectomy Reversal. For guys with mild ED or who just want to optimize their libido, he recommends L-arginine supplements.

L-arginine is an amino acid that supports blood flow through nitric oxide production. Nitric oxide allows blood vessels to open fully and allow more blood flow to come into the penis.

“The penis is a hemodynamic organ. It works on blood flow. There has to be stimulation and a relationship that is functional between the nerves and the blood vessels,” says Dr. Werthman. “Anything that helps nitric oxide stick around longer will cause more blood flow to come in and maybe give a better quality erection.”

If possible, he recommends choosing L-arginine supplements containing L-citrulline (a precursor to L-arginine) or pycnogenol. The latter is an antioxidant made from the bark of a tree and is a powerful antioxidant used often in the fertility world, says Dr. Werthman. In concert with L-arginine, the combo helps to boost erections.

There is one caveat. For the effects to really work, you need to take this supplement on a daily basis. A single scoop the night before a sexual encounter won’t make much of a difference.

“It’s the kind of thing you put into your supplement stack,” says Dr. Werthman. Beyond healthy erections, nitric oxide helps with increasing blood flow all over the body, potentially providing extra benefits to your brain, heart, and muscles if you’re working out.

Buyer Beware: Supplements are not FDA-regulated, and some can get sketchy. Consider getting a product tested and certified by a third-party testing facility to verify the supplement’s safety and quality.

OYSTERS AND CHAMPAGNE get a lot of hype as aphrodisiacs. But Dr. Werthman says the true value is eating foods high in L-arginine. Here are some examples:

Additionally, watermelon is one of the best foods to eat on the day you’re having sex because of its high citrulline content, says Dr. Werthman. So, while spontaneous sex is great, scheduling sex can help you fuel your body (and boner) accordingly.

As for what’s on the don’t eat list? Nothing, but both urologists say it’s best to avoid alcohol before sex. You might gain a little liquid courage, but the buzz kills erections. Alcohol slows down brain signals related to arousal and decreases the ability of blood vessels to trap blood in the penis.

CORTISOL, ALSO KNOWN as your body’s stress hormone, is one of the biggest killers of testosterone and erections. When your body is in fight-or-flight mode, Dr. Werthman says, the last thing it’s thinking about is having sex.

The trademarks of a stressful lifestyle—lack of sleep, long working hours, and a poor diet—can all create barriers to intimacy, says Dr. Miller. Setting aside time to take care of yourself physically will help with performing at your best.

For example, a meditation session or some light stretching can relieve some stress temporarily. You also might want to consider a quick workout. Now, Dr. Werthman warns that a single sweat session won’t do much for your penile health (over time, consistent exercise does support blood flow and cardiovascular health, helping you last longer). But in terms of mental health, the stress-relieving benefits of pushups or a quick jog can help you get amped for the main event. Plus, the endorphins in your body can shake off any pre-sex nerves and make you feel more confident in your body. One study involving over 128,000 people found all types of physical activity—walking, resistance training, Pilates, and yoga—effective in improving anxiety symptoms.

Granted, for some people, sex itself is the stress reliever. But if you tense up thinking about the actual act, Dr. Werthman advises taking it slow. Get out of your head and focus on increasing erotic arousal through kissing and other forms of foreplay, then seeing if you want to go further. “It’s about being comfortable with your partner,” he says. “You want a dynamic where if you get a fail-to-launch situation, they understand. Because it happens—not every encounter leads to a touchdown.”

#4973. At High Point Market, Designers Celebrate a Major Theodore Alexander Milestone With AD

If you were at High Point Market this year, you definitely saw The Chair. The Chippendale-style seat, a towering 15-feet tall, standing sentinel outside Theodore Alexander, the 30-year-old furniture manufacturer known for its craftsmanship and artisan techniques. Naturally, as Market attendees gathered for the Theodore Alexander anniversary party on October 16, the mammoth Pentreath chair served as the entrance’s red-carpet beacon.

After the requisite photo ops with the chair, party co-hosts AD PRO Senior Editor Mel Studach, AD100 Hall of Fame talent Alexa Hampton (Mark Hampton), and AD PRO Directory designers Rasheeda Gray (Gray Space Interiors) and Lisa Shaffer (Lisa & Leroy) welcomed guests into the celebration, which flowed across the showroom’s four floors and rooftop patio. “Since its founding in 1996, Theodore Alexander has built a legacy rooted in craftsmanship, creativity, and a deep respect for the art of furniture making,” said Studach in her opening remarks, which paid homage to company founder Paul Maitland Smith, who passed away earlier this fall at the age of 90. “He proved that exceptional design is as much about the hands that make it as the vision that inspires it. Designer Lisa Shaffer, AD PRO Senior Editor Mel Studach, designer Alexa Hampton, Theodore Alexander President Ed Taplitz, designer Rasheeda Gray, and Theodore Alexander VP of Marketing Sydney Wells Martin.

Guests including Richard Anuszkiewicz (Raith Design), Amber Guyton (Blessed Little Bungalow), Lisa Mende (Lisa Mende Design), and Francis Toumbakaris (Francis Interiors) mingled on the showroom’s amber-lit patio, while others wandered to the lower-level floors where they were invited to view the season’s new collections—Voyager, Greenwich, and Heritage. The Manhasset flagship also offers Theodore Alexander’s made-to-order customization capabilities across every collection.

Over cocktails, wood-fired pizzas, and live music, guests hobnobbed, swapped notes on Market, and celebrated the brand’s remarkable legacy. As they departed, they were gifted that signature Pentreath chair—a miniature keychain version, cast in polished brass—a charming symbol of the decades to come.

#4972. North Korea denies role in $6.3B Binance hack, points finger at US

Pyongyang has pushed back against the FBI’s attribution of the Binance attack, with Kim Yo Jong calling the US allegations politically motivated.

Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denied North Korea’s involvement in the $6.3 billion Binance hack and appeared to suggest, without evidence, that the US could have been behind the theft.

In a statement released via the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Tuesday, Kim rejected the FBI’s attribution of the attack to a North Korean-backed hacking group.

“The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a ‘cyber criminal state’, claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization ‘supported’ by the DPRK was involved in the incident,” said Kim. “But the US assertion is an absurd rhetoric and nothing new.”

She described the allegations as a political provocation intended to damage North Korea’s international standing. The FBI also blamed North Korea for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, an accusation Kim also rejected on Tuesday.

“This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the ‘cyber crime’ incidents whenever they occur on an international scale,” said Kim.

Kim also pointed the finger at the US for involvement in the hack.

“If it carefully examines who will get the large amount of the so-called stolen cryptocurrency when the latter is retrieved, it may get a clue about who is behind the hacking incident,” she said.

The statement provided no evidence connecting Washington to the attack. Cointelegraph reached out to the FBI for comment.

Last week, blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs attributed the Binance attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group with high confidence, citing onchain and offchain intelligence. Other investigators, including Chainalysis and ZachXBT, also linked the theft to North Korean hackers.

TRM Labs pointed to similarities with previous North Korean attacks, including advance preparation, the use of Tornado Cash to fund attacker wallets and the coordinated execution of previously obtained transaction signatures. However, it said the laundering activity differed from the pattern following the Bybit hack.

Onchain investigator ZachXBT also identified a connection between the Binance and Bitget hacks, saying stolen funds from both incidents were commingled at the same address after passing through THORChain. During early investigation into the hack, Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said preliminary findings linked IP addresses to VPN services used “by a certain DPRK group.”

#4971. Extractive Hybridization and the Future of Human Autonomy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Suppose you could press a button that saves you 20 minutes today but carries a small chance of making you less capable five years from now. Would you press it?

Probably. Most of us would. Behavioral economics has spent decades showing that human beings are not the calculating decision-makers imagined in older economic models. We give disproportionate weight to what is immediate. We stick with defaults. We dislike losses more than equivalent gains please us. We take mental shortcuts when choices become complicated. And what people around us are doing gradually shapes what feels normal. These shortcuts allow humans to navigate a world far too complicated to constantly calculate from scratch. They are useful, and they become dangerously important when we introduce a technology that is 1) built around making things easier, faster and increasingly automatic, and 2) fine-tunes to leverage the soft spots of our thinking.

This is where extractive hybridization begins. It describes a trajectory in which artificial intelligence combines with existing human tendencies, incentives and institutions in ways that progressively extract value—from our natural resources; putting a mortgage on the capital that people and planet represent. We are making a bad bargain with our future selves

Consider one of behavioral economics' most familiar findings: we tend to discount the future. A benefit today often feels more valuable than a larger benefit later. The same imbalance applies to costs. The convenience of avoiding a difficult task is immediate; the possible loss of a skill through years of non-use is remote. AI creates thousands of these tiny exchanges. Why struggle for forty minutes to understand a difficult paper when an AI can summarize it in 40 seconds? Why draft the first version yourself? Why remember information that can always be retrieved? Why work through three possible interpretations when the machine can recommend one?

Often, delegating is sensible. The problem is that the transaction is asymmetric. We experience the benefit immediately—the saved time, avoided frustration, finished task—while any cost to competence arrives gradually and is difficult to attribute to yesterday's shortcuts. A 2026 study of cognitive offloading distinguishes between using AI while retaining control of the thinking process and progressively handing the governance of that process to the machine. Both can produce similar immediate benefits; their longer-term relationship with autonomy and competence appears quite different. Beyond asking Can AI do this for me? Should we ponder What happens to me when it repeatedly does?

Defaults matter. Humans disproportionately accept whatever option requires the least intervention. That is why automatically enrolling employees in pensions can dramatically change saving behaviour without removing anyone's freedom to opt out. Now consider the progression of generative AI. Over the past three years it has been gradually embedded in email, search engines, operating systems, classrooms, and workplaces. The outcome is that artificial assistance has shifted from being an isolated crutch to the default configuration. Instead of deciding whether to use AI, we may increasingly have to decide when to override it.

It is a small difference, with big consequences.

Experiments found that the way individuals evaluate AI-generated suggestions can produce systematic errors. Human oversight does not automatically solve the problem simply because a person remains formally “in the loop.” The quality of that human judgment matters. More strikingly, the interaction with biased AI could make humans more biased over time. Participants also underestimated how strongly the algorithm had influenced them. The machine was not simply reflecting human bias; interaction resulted in a hybrid feedback loop in favor of the artificial inject. As we are moving toward a future in which AI is increasingly pervasive, it is crucial to be aware of the lopsided influence that algorithms have on our judgement.

Here Extractive Hybridization becomes more subtle. Algorithms learn partly from traces of human behaviour: what we click, watch, buy, ignore and share. Yet behavioral economics tells us that observed behaviour does not always reveal what people genuinely prefer. Sometimes we click because we are tired, distracted, angry, or acting automatically. Algorithms learn from our choices. But when our impulsive behaviour becomes training material for the environment that shapes our next choice, it results in the best-case scenario in the automation of automatism, and in the worst-case scenario in a setting where our biases are the default.

The loop is bound to become circular: We behave automatically => The system learns from that behaviour => It reorganizes our choices accordingly => Those choices encourage more of the behaviour it learned from.

Nobody needs to intend the outcome; and yet the accumulation of short-sighted choices, creates the tragedy of the commons – where the majority suffer in the long-term because a critical mass benefited in the short term. This is the micro layer of the "Hybrid Tipping Zone": a period in which repeated human–machine interactions begin to trace behavioural tracks. Like a path through deep snow, every traveller makes the established route easier for the next.

The deepest driver of today's extractive economy is a mindset that repeatedly equates more with better, faster with progress, and easier with desirable. AI puts that mindset on amphetamines. If success means maximizing output, AI can generate more. If success means capturing attention, it can personalize persuasion. If success means maximizing consumption, it can predict desires and nudge purchases. Technology amplifies. Which makes our signals precious. They are where the alternative to the status quo begins.

Hybrid flourishing does not require humans to become perfectly rational, nor AI to become perfectly aligned. It starts with recognizing the peculiarities of both. We can design AI to introduce reflection where convenience would otherwise remove it. Instead of immediately answering, a learning system might first ask what the student thinks. Decision-support tools can expose uncertainty and counterarguments rather than presenting a frictionless recommendation. Systems designed to challenge people's reasoning can reduce over-reliance, by injecting friction. That extra effort may sometimes be exactly the point.

The crucial distinction is between friction that wastes human potential and friction that develops it. That makes Extractive Hybridization fundamentally a story about mindsets. AI will amplify our ability to pursue objectives, but it cannot decide which objectives deserve pursuing. If we enter the hybrid age carrying forward short-termism, automatic behaviour and an unquestioned preference for more, faster and easier, artificial intelligence can scale those tendencies magnificently.

If we become more conscious of our current priorities, the same technology can help us do something considerably more interesting: notice our biases, widen our field of vision, explore consequences and make better choices for people and planet.

Before asking what kind of AI we want, we may need to ask what kind of human we want it to amplify.

#4969. Bijan Robinson Has a Secret Weapon. It’s Not What You Think.

The Falcons star approaches this area of health with the same discipline as his game.

BIJAN ROBINSON DOESN’T lack confidence. The Atlanta Falcons running back has been one of the best players at his position even before his days in the NFL, when he was a top back at the University of Texas and a number one-rated recruit going into college. He’s not afraid to show it, either. “If you know me, [you know] I smile a lot,” he tells Men’s Health.

As much as he has depended on his smile to project his self-assurance, Robinson didn’t always feel the best about his teeth. He recalls some slightly awkward stages in his younger years. “When I was a kid, more middle school, I was still kind of growing into my teeth,” he says. “I had two teeth that would kind of twist in a little bit.”

For lots of guys, the state of their smile is a huge concern. But Robinson didn’t want to go through the trouble of getting braces to address the issue. “I was still trying to avoid having a wire on my teeth, because I thought that it would limit me from eating certain things, trying to keep it straight.” Robinson grew into his smile, and didn’t worry as much about his teeth as he became one of the most celebrated football players in the country.

But when he eventually entered the NFL, he realized how a small fix could make a big difference for his professional image. Robinson partnered with Invisalign and began wearing the clear aligners to straighten out that little twist in his smile.

“You're in front of a camera a lot in interviews and even just talking to people [at] events,” he says. “Having [my] smile is not only a confidence booster for myself, but the other I'm talking to—it makes them more engaged in the conversation. They see you take care of yourself.”

Robinson says he wears the aligners everywhere—even with his helmet on in practice and in games. He says a traditional mouthguard makes it difficult for him to breathe, and his conditioning is what gives him an edge as a back who can score out of the backfield as a runner and receiver. (Invisalign reps clarified it should not be used as a mouthguard).

Overall, Robinson appreciates how he’s able to make his oral health another aspect of the self-discipline and self-improvement practices that have helped him to be such a standout player. Like his workouts and skill-position drills, he takes it seriously. His smile is also his responsibility. “I'm not only representing myself,” he says. “I'm representing the Falcons, my family—everybody.”

#4968. South Korea urges exchanges to boost cold storage after Binance hack

South Korean crypto exchanges are already required to hold at least 80% of customer crypto in cold wallets, but the regulator is urging more.

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has urged domestic crypto exchanges to increase the proportion of assets held in cold wallets after the $6.3 billion attack on Binance last week.

In a statement Monday, the FSC said it held an emergency meeting with the Financial Supervisory Service, the Financial Security Institute, the Digital Asset eXchange Alliance (DAXA) and major crypto service providers to review the impact of the Binance hack on South Korea’s crypto market and review exchanges’ security measures.

The FSC said it reviewed exchanges’ IT access controls, wallet withdrawal approval and signing procedures, and administrator privileges. It also urged providers to increase the proportion of assets held in offline cold wallets.

Attackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance’s internet-connected hot wallets last week, moving most of the funds in about 20 minutes, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. Binance has said the vast majority of users’ assets are held in cold storage.

South Korean law already requires exchanges to hold at least 80% of users’ crypto assets in cold storage, though cold wallet holdings vary considerably among South Korea’s major exchanges.

At the end of September, Upbit’s cold wallet ratio stood at 99.17%, followed by Bithumb at 94.76% and Coinone at 85%, according to Financial Supervisory Service data cited by local media. Digital X, formerly Korbit, and GOPAX reported ratios of 82.79% and 80.54%, respectively.

Related: North Korea denies role in $6.3B Binance hack, points finger at US

The FSC also urged providers to continuously monitor deposits and withdrawals, secure additional incident response personnel and promptly report and share information about unusual access attempts.

Operators were also asked to set aside additional reserves and implement other security measures that could be introduced immediately to prevent similar breaches. The regulator said it would continue working with relevant agencies and the industry to prevent further attacks and limit potential damage.

Cointelegraph reached out to Upbit, Bithumb, Coinone, Digital X and GOPAX for comment.

The FSC’s warning comes as the Bank of Korea separately surveys 18 banks and 13 brokerages about their exposure to crypto-related risks, including major exchange hacks and prolonged market downturns. The central bank’s review began before the Binance attack.

#4967. Where Does Brock Purdy Live? Exploring the Homes of the San Francisco 49ers Quarterback

He spends plenty of time at Levi Stadium as the quarterback of the San Francisco 49ers, but where does Brock Purdy live when he’s off the field? The football player was born and raised in Queen Creek, Arizona, and played football at Perry High School in nearby Gilbert. While Purdy left Arizona in 2018 to play at Iowa State University, he’s still fond of his home state. “I love the state of Arizona and everyone that’s been a part of my life,” he told reporters ahead of the 2024 Super Bowl. “And obviously, I’m trying to represent them as best as I can for as long as my career goes.”

At Iowa State, Purdy was a three-time All-Big 12 quarterback and was the winningest quarterback in the school’s history. The University’s Midwest environment suited Purdy. “My favorite part is the people, just because of how down-to-earth and real everyone is,” he told the Iowa Stater in 2024. “Everyone wants to help each other out. There’s no selfishness. I don’t know what it is about the culture in Iowa, but everybody just loves one another authentically. And when you go back, you feel that every time.” Purdy also met his future wife, Jenna, his freshman year at Iowa State. The couple got engaged in 2023 and tied the knot back in Iowa in 2024.

In 2022, the San Francisco 49ers selected Purdy as the final pick of the NFL Draft. This pick typically earns the harsh nickname Mr. Irrelevant, but Purdy quickly proved the moniker wrong, becoming starting quarterback in his rookie season. Now in his fifth season with the 49ers, Purdy is also building a successful life off the field. Read on to learn about Brock Purdy’s homes over the years.

Teammates—and onetime roommates—Alfredo Gutierrez, Nick Zakelj, and Purdy in the locker room in 2022

At the beginning of his NFL career, Purdy lived more like a recent college grad than a pro football player. During his rookie year, Purdy shared a house with offensive linemen Alfredo Gutierrez and Nick Zakelj. The trio even gave out a Christmas card from the household to teammates. In an interview with NBC Sports Bay Area, Gutierrez revealed that Purdy did most of the cooking out of the three and that they spent downtime watching football, movies, and playing Mario Super Slugger.

By 2023, Purdy had only one roommate: Zakelj. “So he and I are still splitting rent,” Purdy told the TODAY Show. “I still drive my Toyota Sequoia. Other than that, it’s pretty simple.”

Purdy with his wife, Jenna, and daughter, Millie Joleen, in 2025. They now have a second child on the way.

Purdy left his shared home in 2024 when he married his wife, Jenna. They now live in a rental home in the Bay Area with their daughter, Millie Joleen, who was born in July 2025. The couple announced in July 2026 that they would soon be welcoming a second child.

The couple focused on making the home family-friendly, adding plenty of storage for their daughter’s toys, and durable furniture for hosting. “Becoming new parents, we really wanted this house to feel like a home where our family is going to continue to grow,” Jenna said in a video unveiling the couple’s living room and bedroom makeovers, which they worked on with Pottery Barn.

In May 2025, Purdy signed a five-year, $265 million deal with the 49ers, making him the fifth-highest-paid quarterback in the league. The hefty pay raise led Purdy to start his real estate portfolio. His teammate, 49ers tight end George Kittle, revealed on a podcast in June of that year that Purdy had purchased a home in Nashville.

Purdy with teammate George Kittle in 2025

“He did purchase a house in Nashville, Tennessee,” Kittle said. “He will be kind of a neighbor to me at some point. That will be pretty fun, because I’ll have a quarterback that can throw to me all the time, that’s actually on my team.” That summer, Purdy was seen training at Kittle’s football compound in Nashville.

Fleece is a soft, synthetic fabric usually made from a polyester blend, often mixed with spandex, nylon, or cotton. Designed to mimic wool's insulating properties, fleece is lighter, more breathable, and dries faster, making it ideal for staying warm. Plus, fleece wicks away moisture and dries quickly, keeping you cozy even if you’re caught in rain or snow. Think of it like wearing a warm hug on a cold day.

When it comes to fleece leggings, the fabric blend is key. Most leggings are made from a mix of polyester and spandex, which delivers the perfect blend of warmth, stretch, and comfort. We’ll give you a quick breakdown of why these materials are key here:

Polyester traps heat, making it an ideal blend for staying warm without bulk. Compared to natural fibers like cotton, polyester dries quickly. WH editors love wearing polyester-fleece leggings on long walks since they stay warm without making you feel sweaty. It’s super lightweight yet strong, meaning you won’t feel like the material is clinging to your body. Polyester also helps leggings retain their shape over time, so stretching, sagging, and pilling are likely a thing of the past.

Nylon is a popular material in fleece leggings because of its strength, flexibility, and smooth texture. It resists wear and tear, which helps keep leggings looking brand new after every wash. Nylon also offers water resistance, which is key for outdoor activities in light rain or snow.

Spandex (also known as elastane or Lycra) is the go-to fabric for stretch and flexibility. It fits snugly and moves with you, giving you maximum comfort during high-impact activities like yoga, running, and dance. While it’s not as durable on its own, spandex is often blended with other fabrics (like nylon or polyester) to create leggings that are both stretchy and long-lasting.

Here’s the thing: Fleece leggings with thicker fabric may feel more restrictive than traditional leggings, so if you plan to wear them for high-impact activities, opting for a bigger size might be best. Look for four-way stretch fabrics like spandex for flexibility and comfort. If you're between sizes, choose based on your desired fit—size down for a sculpted look (read: tighter) or up for a relaxed, lounge-friendly feel.

Fleece leggings are perfect for workouts, offering warmth and insulation while keeping the stretch and comfort you need for full range of motion. “The leggings should have a good amount of stretch while fitting snugly, and maintaining their shape throughout the day,” says fashion designer Kadeem Alphanso Fyffe. Look for features like a wide, high-rise waistband for a secure fit.

As writers who've tried more than our fair share of leggings, we know what it takes to make a great pair. To earn a place on this list, these fleece leggings had to meet strict criteria. We analyzed everything from fabric quality and warmth to stretch, fit, and breathability. Were they soft and supportive? Did they hold their shape after multiple washes? Could they withstand the elements without pilling or wearing thin? We examined every seam, ensuring each recommendation is a worthy investment for your winter wardrobe and beyond.

We also consulted two style experts, who shared their favorite pairs and provided insight on what to consider when shopping for fleece leggings. They emphasized that materials, stretch, and overall style matter, since they can make or break a pair of leggings (and pants, for that matter).

#4965. Binance begins second withdrawal phase, exchange outflows slow

The exchange says additional assets will become available for withdrawal from 04:00 UTC on Tuesday as security checks are completed, following an initial reopening on Sunday.

Binance plans to begin a second phase of cryptocurrency withdrawals on Tuesday, as data shows withdrawal volumes have started to stabilize following last week’s $6.3 billion hack.

Withdrawals for additional assets are scheduled to resume progressively from 04:00 UTC on Tuesday, according to Binance’s latest recovery notice. The rollout follows an initial reopening on Nov. 1.

“Like phase one, reopening will roll out progressively across the assets as security and readiness checks are completed,” said Binance.

The exchange said it was prioritizing tokens based on user demand over the past week. Deposits remain available.

Networks part of the second phase of withdrawals include Binance Smart Chain, Ethereum, Solana, XRP Ledger, Sui, Arbitrum, Optimism, Tron and Base, according to Binance.

Binance’s list of assets planned for withdrawal. Source: Binance

On Monday, Binance said it also reopened withdrawals for several fiat currencies, including the US dollar, United Arab Emirates dirham, Vietnamese dong, Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah, adding to a list of 23 other currencies already available for withdrawal.

Data from DefiLlama shows outflows from the crypto exchange have slowed since Sunday, with net outflows on Monday at $2.57 billion, compared to $6.1 billion the day before.

In a separate security reminder, Binance warned that scammers could exploit the phased reopening by impersonating the exchange and offering accelerated withdrawals, sell priority processing, help users claim compensation or direct them to move assets into a purported “Binance vault,” the exchange said.

“Anyone promising to expedite it for a fee is scamming you,” Binance said.
